title: The three jobs of money
description: Money is whatever works as a medium of exchange (a way to pay), a unit of account (a measure of value) and a store of value (a way to save).

facts.text: Money does three jobs: it is a medium of exchange, a unit of account and a store of value.
As a medium of exchange, money sits between buyer and seller: people accept it as payment so they can spend it on something else.
As a unit of account, money is the common ruler for measuring value, so prices are stated and compared in one unit, usually a currency.
As a store of value, money can be saved and used later.

title: Cigarettes as money in a POW camp
description: In a WWII prisoner-of-war camp described by R. A. Radford in 1945, cigarettes became the currency and did all three jobs of money.

facts.text: Economist R. A. Radford, a prisoner of war in World War II, described his camp's economy in a 1945 paper.
In Radford's camp, cigarettes became the normal currency: everyone, including non-smokers, would sell for cigarettes and use them to buy later.
Trade in Radford's camp started as direct barter before cigarettes took over as currency.
Camp prices were quoted in cigarettes: prisoners called out offers like 'cheese for seven', and laundry cost two cigarettes a garment.
Prisoners held reserves of cigarettes, but cigarettes were also smoked, so when deliveries stopped, stocks ran out and prices fell.

title: Barter and the double coincidence of wants
description: Barter is trading goods or services directly; it only works when each side wants what the other offers.

facts.text: Barter is trading one good or service directly for another, without money.
Barter needs a double coincidence of wants: each person must want something the other can provide.
Without money, a car mechanic who wanted food would have to find a farmer with a broken car.

title: Barter has no common measure
description: Barter has no single unit for measuring value and makes saving for later hard.

facts.text: Barter with no established measures has no underlying index of value: each exchange stands virtually on its own.
Barter makes it hard to buy things later with perishable goods, like a farmer hoping to pay for a tractor in six months with fresh strawberries.

title: Barter in history
description: No society that ran purely on barter has ever been described; barter tends to appear between acquaintances and when money runs short.

facts.text: Economists since Adam Smith have told a story in which barter came first and money replaced it once people saw it was more efficient.
In 1985, anthropologist Caroline Humphrey concluded that no pure barter economy has ever been described.
Barter tends to take place between people who know one another.
In Radford's camp, when cigarette deliveries were interrupted, trade became increasingly a matter of barter.

title: Cowrie shell money
description: Cowrie shells served as money in parts of Africa and Asia because they were small, durable and hard to fake.

facts.text: Cowrie shells were small, light, durable and difficult to counterfeit.
Cowrie shells served as money in Africa, in places until the late 19th century.
In China, strings of cowrie shells were used in royal gifts and payments from around 1000 BCE.
Many modern Chinese characters about money, such as those for buy, loan and tax, include the ancient symbol for a cowrie shell.

title: Salt money
description: In Ethiopia, bars of salt served as money for centuries; salt was useful as well as accepted.

facts.text: In Ethiopia, bars of salt were used as money for many hundreds of years, until the 1930s.
Salt made good money partly because it is a commodity that nearly everyone needs.

title: Yap's stone money
description: On Yap, large stone discs quarried on Palau served as money, changing owners by shared agreement without moving.

facts.text: Yap's stone money discs were quarried on Palau, hundreds of kilometers away, and carried back across the sea.
The largest Yap stones are more than 3.5 meters across.
Large Yap stones usually stayed put when they changed hands; everyone simply knew who the new owner was.
According to Yap tradition, recorded by visitor William Furness, one stone sank in a storm on its way home, and islanders agreed it still counted as its owners' wealth.

title: The first coins
description: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in modern Turkey, around 650 BCE; coinage also arose separately in China.

facts.text: The first coins were probably made in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, around 650 BCE.
Lydia's first coins were made of electrum, a natural mix of gold and silver, to strict weight standards.
Many early Lydian coins carried a lion's head, which seems to have been a royal symbol.
Lydia was the first place to mint separate gold and silver coins; they are often credited to the legendarily wealthy King Croesus, but were probably made before and after his reign too.
Electrum's worth was harder to calculate than pure gold's or silver's because it mixed metals.
The idea of gold and silver coinage spread rapidly around the Mediterranean.
China's earliest coins were cast in bronze in the shapes of tools such as spades and knives.
Most historians think coinage arose in China independently of Lydia.

title: What a coin's stamp did
description: A coin's stamp showed that an authority stood behind a standard weight of metal, so it no longer had to be weighed in every deal.

facts.text: Before coins, traders paid with rings or bars of precious metal that had to be weighed and checked in every deal.
Coins with standard weights removed the need to weigh metal in every deal.
Stamping a piece of precious metal marked it as official money that the state was willing to accept as payment.

title: Why metal made good money
description: Metal suits money because it is portable, does not perish and is hard to counterfeit.

facts.text: To work as money, coins need to be portable, non-perishable and hard to counterfeit, which is why they are made of metal.

title: Paper money in China
description: Paper money began in China, from Tang-era flying money to Song-era notes in Sichuan, where heavy iron coins made paper convenient.

facts.text: In Tang dynasty China (618–907), merchants used paper drafts called 'flying money' (feiqian) instead of carrying heavy coins over long distances.
Historians differ on flying money: the British Museum calls it the first paper money, while others describe it as drafts for moving funds.
In 11th-century Sichuan, heavy iron coins led people to leave their coins on deposit and use paper certificates instead.
Around 1023, the Song government took over issuing Sichuan's paper certificates.
The Song-era notes of Sichuan, called jiaozi, are widely described as the world's first paper currency.

title: Paper money reaches Europe
description: Marco Polo described Chinese paper money in the 13th century; Europe's first banknotes came from Sweden's Stockholms Banco in 1661.

facts.text: Marco Polo gave one of the earliest European accounts of Chinese paper money after his travels in the 13th century.
Europe's first real banknotes were issued in 1661 by Stockholms Banco in Sweden.
Sweden's first banknotes caught on because they were more convenient than heavy, cumbersome copper coins.
Stockholms Banco failed after the public lost confidence in its notes.

title: Fiat money
description: Fiat money has no value of its own and no commodity backing; a government declares it legal tender.

facts.text: Fiat money has no intrinsic value and no commodity backing; a government declares it legal tender.
US paper money carries the statement: 'This note is legal tender for all debts, public and private.'
Today's US dollars are fiat money, not backed by gold or any other commodity.

title: Money runs on trust
description: Money is valuable because people trust that others will accept it; when that trust goes, its value goes too.

facts.text: In 2025, printing a US $100 note cost about 11 cents: 11.3 cents in paper, ink, labor and direct overhead.
The only backing of fiat money is people's shared faith and trust that it has value.
Money works because people believe that it will.
In 1991, economist Milton Friedman used Yap's stone money to show how important unquestioned belief is in monetary matters, including for our own money.

title: The gold standard
description: Under a gold standard, a currency's unit is fixed to a set amount of gold and paper money can be exchanged for it.

facts.text: Under a gold standard, a currency's unit is a fixed quantity of gold, or is kept at the value of one.
Britain adopted the gold standard in 1821, and by the 1870s other big economies, including Germany and France, had followed.
Under the US gold standard, the Federal Reserve had to convert dollars into gold at a fixed price.

title: Leaving the gold standard
description: Countries left gold because its supply limited their money; the US ended its last gold link, for foreign governments, in 1971.

facts.text: The supply of newly mined gold isn't closely related to how much money a growing economy needs, which made the gold standard inflexible.
World War I pushed countries to suspend gold convertibility, and after the Great Depression, no country kept a full gold standard by 1937.
In 1933, the US stopped converting currency and bank deposits into gold coins and bars.
After World War II, under the Bretton Woods system, other currencies were fixed to the dollar, and dollars were convertible to gold at $35 an ounce.
On August 15, 1971, President Nixon closed the gold window: foreign governments could no longer exchange their dollars for gold.
Nixon said he had directed the Treasury to 'suspend temporarily' the dollar's convertibility into gold.
After 1971, the Bretton Woods system soon ended, and the international monetary system in effect became a fiat one.

title: Money as bank deposits
description: Most money today is bank deposits: records of what banks owe their customers, not physical cash.

facts.text: In the UK, 97% of the money held by the public is bank deposits rather than notes and coins (Bank of England, 2014); the other 3% is currency.
A bank deposit is an IOU from the bank: a record of what the bank owes its customer.
Money today is a special kind of IOU that everyone in the economy trusts.
Most people now receive their pay as bank deposits, and many never swap those deposits back into cash.

title: Paying by changing records
description: A card payment changes banks' records: the payer's balance goes down and the seller's goes up.

facts.text: When you pay a shop by debit card, the banks reduce your deposit and increase the shop's; no cash changes hands.
In the early 1930s, the New York Fed transferred gold to the Bank of France by moving it into drawers in its own vault labeled as French property; the gold never crossed the ocean.
Friedman noted that much of what people count as wealth, such as entries in a bank account, is never directly seen by its owners.

title: What a cryptocurrency is
description: Cryptocurrencies such as bitcoin are digital tokens created and tracked by a network of computers, with no central issuer.

facts.text: Bitcoin was proposed in October 2008 in a paper by Satoshi Nakamoto, a pseudonym for an unknown person or group, and launched in 2009.
Nakamoto designed bitcoin to work as a medium of exchange without relying on financial institutions or governments.
Bitcoin is a digital token with no physical form, created and tracked by a network of computers rather than issued by a bank, company or government.
Cryptocurrencies are named for their heavy use of cryptography.

title: The blockchain ledger
description: A blockchain is a shared, tamper-evident ledger in which each block of transactions is linked to the one before.

facts.text: A blockchain is a digital ledger of transactions shared across a network, usually with no central authority.
Each block carries a cryptographic link (a hash) to the block before, so changing an old block changes every later one, which makes tampering easy to detect.
Crypto is spent by signing with a secret private key; if the key is lost, the coins it controls are lost, because the key can't be regenerated.
Anthropologist Scott Fitzpatrick and finance professor Stephen McKeon have compared Yap's shared oral record of stone ownership to a blockchain.

title: Why crypto prices swing
description: Bitcoin's price is set by supply and demand; with a nearly fixed supply and no issuer steadying it, the price swings sharply.

facts.text: Bitcoin's value has skyrocketed and tumbled dramatically within the space of a few days.
Bitcoin's price is set by global supply and demand.
The number of bitcoins is capped at slightly less than 21 million.
Bitcoin's more-or-less fixed supply cannot respond to changes in demand, so, as under the gold standard, its price is bound to swing more than the dollar's.
Some supporters see bitcoin's fixed supply as a hedge against inflation; critics point to its drastic price volatility.
The European Central Bank argues that bitcoin is too unstable to be a reliable store of value.

title: Six traits of useful money
description: Useful money is durable, portable, divisible, uniform, limited in supply and acceptable.

facts.text: Economists list six traits of useful money: durability, portability, divisibility, uniformity, limited supply and acceptability.
Yap's stones are durable, scarce and accepted, but not portable or uniform.
A US $20 bill scores well on all six traits of useful money.

title: The factors of production
description: Economists group the resources that make goods and services into land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship.

facts.text: Economists group the resources used to produce goods and services into four factors of production: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship.
In economics, land means any natural resource used to produce goods and services, such as water, oil or forests.
In economics, capital means the tools, machinery and buildings used to produce goods and services, such as hammers, computers and delivery vans.
An entrepreneur combines the other factors of production (land, labor and capital) to earn a profit.

title: Four kinds of income
description: Land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurship earns profit; wages are most people's main income.

facts.text: Each factor of production earns its own kind of income: land earns rent, labor earns wages, capital earns interest and entrepreneurship earns profit.
Profit is the income left over after all costs, including wages, rent and interest, have been paid.
Wages, the income earned by labor, are the largest source of income for most people.

title: Gross and net pay
description: Gross pay is what you earn before deductions; net (take-home) pay is what you receive after them.

facts.text: Gross pay is what you earn from your wages or salary before any deductions are taken out.
Net pay, or take-home pay, is what you actually receive after tax withholding and other deductions are taken out.

title: Paycheck deductions
description: Employers withhold payroll taxes and income tax, and may deduct retirement or health contributions, before pay arrives.

facts.text: Employers withhold part of employees' pay to cover payroll taxes and income tax and send it to the government; money may also be deducted for retirement or health benefits.
US payroll taxes, called FICA, take 6.2% of an employee's pay for Social Security and 1.45% for Medicare: 7.65% in total.
On a $1,000 paycheck, 7.65% payroll taxes come to $76.50: $62.00 for Social Security and $14.50 for Medicare.
Employers also pay their own matching share of Social Security and Medicare taxes, on top of what they withhold from employees.
Federal income tax rates are the same across the US, and some states and localities also have their own income taxes.

title: What a budget is
description: A budget is a written monthly plan: list expenses, note income, subtract, then track what you actually spend.

facts.text: The word budget comes from the Old French bougette, a small leather bag; its money sense dates from 1733, from a treasury minister keeping his financial plans in a bag.
A budget is a plan you write down to decide how you will spend your money each month.
To make a budget, list your bills and other expenses, write down your monthly income, then subtract expenses from income; the result should be more than zero.
If income minus expenses comes out below zero, you are spending more money than you make and need to change something in the budget.
A budget is used every month: plan at the start, write down what you spend each day, and check at the end of the month whether you spent what you planned.

title: The 50/30/20 rule
description: A common guideline: 50% of after-tax income to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to saving or paying down debt.

facts.text: The 50/30/20 rule puts 50% of after-tax income toward needs, 30% toward wants and 20% toward saving or paying down debt.
Elizabeth Warren and her daughter Amelia Warren Tyagi popularized the 50/30/20 rule in their book All Your Worth.
The 50/30/20 rule is meant as a general guideline for dividing up a paycheck, not a precise law.

title: Needs and wants
description: Needs are essential to survival and basic living; wants are for enjoyment. A need can come in a want-sized version.

facts.text: Needs are expenses essential to survival and basic living, such as food, shelter, clothing and utilities; wants are things you desire for enjoyment or lifestyle.
Within a need there can be a want: you need food, but dining out every night is a want.

title: Needs set by custom
description: Adam Smith counted as necessaries whatever local custom made shameful to go without, so the line between needs and wants moves with time and place.

facts.text: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith defined necessaries as not only what is needed to support life, but whatever local custom makes it shameful for respectable people to be without.

Smith noted that a linen shirt is not strictly necessary for life, since the ancient Greeks and Romans lived comfortably without linen, yet a respectable day-labourer of his time would be ashamed to appear in public without one.

Smith wrote that custom made leather shoes a necessity in England for men and women, in Scotland for men but not women, and in France for neither, where people could go in wooden shoes or barefoot without shame.

title: Opportunity cost
description: Every choice costs the value of the next best alternative you give up, including time and lost earnings.

facts.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative: what you give up when you make a choice.
Every choice has an opportunity cost: if you sleep through a class, the opportunity cost is the learning you miss.

College has out-of-pocket costs such as tuition and books, plus the opportunity cost of earnings you give up because you cannot work a paying job while in class and studying; that opportunity cost exceeds the money cost.
A student who spends 3 hours and $20 at the movies the night before an exam gives up study time as well as the money.

title: No such thing as a free lunch
description: Saloons once gave free lunch to drink buyers; the saying that no lunch is free became an economic maxim.

facts.text: In the 1800s and early 1900s, American saloons offered a free lunch to customers who bought drinks.
The saying that there is no such thing as a free lunch appeared as an economic maxim by 1938, and Milton Friedman used a version of it as a book title in 1975.

title: Pricing cues
description: Shoppers rarely know what a price should be, so cues like prices ending in 9 and sale signs sway them.

facts.text: In a catalog study by Eric Anderson and Duncan Simester, raising a dress's price from $34 to $39 increased demand by about a third.
For most items, shoppers don't have an accurate sense of what the price should be, so they rely on cues such as sale signs and prices ending in 9.
In catalog tests, adding the word "sale" beside a price increased demand by more than 50%.

title: The decoy effect
description: Adding a third, worse option can steer people toward one of the original two.

facts.text: The decoy effect is when adding a third, less attractive option changes how people choose between the original two.

title: How a card payment travels
description: A card payment links the cardholder, the merchant, the merchant's bank (acquirer) and the card issuer through a card network: authorize, then settle.

facts.text: A Visa or Mastercard payment involves four parties: the cardholder, the bank that issued the card, the merchant and the merchant's bank, called the acquirer.
To authorize a card payment, the acquirer sends the request through the card network to the cardholder's issuing bank, which checks that the account is valid.
The acquirer then settles the purchase, paying the merchant's account with money from the issuer, minus the interchange fee and its own service fees.

title: Who pays card fees
description: Merchants pay a fee on card sales, mostly interchange to the card issuer, set by the networks; the cost is passed on in prices, including to cash users.

facts.text: Merchants pay a merchant discount fee on card sales, and most of it goes from the acquirer to the card issuer as an interchange fee.
Card networks set interchange fees, which for credit cards generally range from about 1 to 3 percent of the purchase price.
Merchants generally pass the costs of accepting cards on to all their customers through higher retail prices.
A 2010 Boston Fed study found that because merchants generally charge card and cash users the same price, cash users in effect pay part of the cost of card fees and rewards.

title: Forgotten subscriptions
description: People underestimate recurring subscription spending and often forget charges they no longer use.

facts.text: In a 2022 C+R Research survey of 1,000 US consumers, people guessed they spent $86 a month on subscriptions; itemized, the average was $219.
In the same survey, 74% said recurring subscription charges were easy to forget, and 42% had stopped using a subscription but forgot they were still paying for it.

title: Small costs over a year
description: A small recurring cost looks small month by month; added up over a year it becomes a big number, and a big opportunity cost.

facts.text: The survey's gap of $133 a month between guessed and actual subscription spending adds up to $1,596 over 12 months.
Spending $5 a day more on a bought lunch than a lunch from home adds up to $1,250 over 250 workdays, perhaps the cost of a decent vacation.
Describing a small daily cost by what it adds up to, such as "a nice vacation" instead of "$5 a day", might lead you to make different choices.

title: Four signs of a scam
description: Scammers pretend to be someone you know, claim a problem or prize, pressure you to act now, and demand a specific way to pay.

facts.text: No real business or government agency will ever tell you to buy a gift card to pay them.
The FTC lists four signs of a scam: scammers pretend to be from an organization you know, say there is a problem or a prize, pressure you to act immediately, and tell you to pay in a specific way.
Scammers often pretend to be contacting you from the government or from a business you know, such as a utility or tech company.
Scammers say there is a problem, such as money you owe or an account that needs verifying, or a prize you have won.
Scammers pressure you to act immediately, before you have time to think, sometimes with threats such as arrest or a lawsuit.
Scammers tell you to pay in a specific way: with cryptocurrency, by wiring money, through a payment app or with a gift card.

title: How much scams cost
description: In 2024 people reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud to the FTC, most of it through bank transfers and crypto.

facts.text: People reported losing more than $12.5 billion to fraud in 2024, according to FTC data.
Impostor scams were the most commonly reported type of scam in 2024.
In 2024, people reported losing more money to scams paid by bank transfer or cryptocurrency than by all other payment methods combined.

title: Engel's law
description: The lower a household's income, the bigger the share of it spent on food; richer households spend more dollars but a smaller share.

facts.text: Statistician Ernst Engel, studying the budgets of 153 Belgian families, found that the lower a family's income, the greater the share of it spent on food.
In 2024, the lowest-income fifth of US households spent 33.0% of before-tax income on food; the highest-income fifth spent 6.4%.
In 2024, the highest-income fifth of US households spent more dollars on food ($16,989 on average) than the lowest-income fifth ($5,498), but a much smaller share of income.

title: Money changers and the first banks
description: The word bank comes from the Italian banco, the bench of medieval money changers, who began taking deposits and lending them out.

facts.text: The word bank comes from the Italian banco (Old Italian banca), the bench or table at which medieval money changers did business.
Medieval Lombard money changers mainly exchanged coins for foreign merchants and travelers, then began taking deposits and lending them out.

title: Banks as intermediaries
description: A bank accepts deposits and makes loans, standing between savers and borrowers.

facts.text: A bank accepts deposits and makes loans, acting as a financial intermediary between savers who deposit money and borrowers who take loans.
With a bank, savers can deposit spare money instead of looking for an individual who will borrow it and repay them later.

title: How banks earn: the spread
description: A bank charges borrowers a higher interest rate than it pays depositors; the difference covers costs and profit.

facts.text: A bank's business relies on charging a higher interest rate on loans than it pays on deposits; the difference, the spread, covers its costs and profit.

title: Bank lending creates money
description: When a bank makes a loan it creates a matching new deposit; most money today is created this way, and repaying loans destroys it.

facts.text: Whenever a bank makes a loan, it credits the borrower's account with a matching new deposit, creating new money.
When a bank lends to someone taking out a mortgage to buy a house, it doesn't hand over banknotes; it credits their account with a deposit the size of the mortgage.
Because deposits are created when loans are approved, some economists have called them 'fountain pen money', made at the stroke of a banker's pen.
Most money in the modern economy is created by commercial banks making loans.
Rather than lending out deposits that savers place with them, banks create deposits by lending: the reverse of the order typically described in textbooks.
Repaying a bank loan destroys money: the deposit that lending created disappears.

title: Limits on bank money creation
description: Banks cannot create money without limit: they must lend profitably and manage risk, regulation constrains them, and central bank interest rates are the ultimate limit.

facts.text: Banks can't create money without limit: they must lend profitably and manage risk, regulation constrains them, and central bank interest rates are the ultimate limit.

title: Interest: the price of borrowing
description: Interest is the price a borrower pays a lender for the use of money, usually stated as a rate; lenders charge it for giving up money now and for taking risk.

facts.text: Interest is the price or fee a borrower pays a lender for the use of money; it can be stated as a rate.
At an interest rate of 5% a year, borrowing $100 for a year costs $5 in interest.
If someone would pay $95 today for a promise of $100 in a year, the $5 difference is interest: payment for giving up the use of money now.
A bank or credit union may also pay you interest when you deposit money in certain accounts.

title: Interest in ancient Mesopotamia
description: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code in the 18th century BCE, set interest rates: 20% on silver and more on riskier barley loans.

facts.text: Mesopotamian laws, including Hammurabi's code in the 18th century BCE, set interest rates on loans: 20% for silver and a higher rate for barley.
Barley loans, usually made to the poor, were seen as riskier than silver loans, which is why the law allowed them a higher rate.
Hammurabi's interest laws (18th century BCE) came more than 1,000 years before Lydia's first coins (around 650 BCE).

title: Compound interest
description: Compound interest is paid on the original amount plus the interest already earned, so growth speeds up over time.

facts.text: Simple interest is calculated only on the original amount; compound interest is calculated on the original amount plus the interest already earned.
On a debt, compounding means interest is charged on the unpaid balance plus earlier unpaid interest, which is how credit card debt can balloon.

title: The Rule of 72
description: Dividing 72 by an annual interest rate estimates how many years compounding takes to double money.

facts.text: The Rule of 72 estimates how long money takes to double with compounding: divide 72 by the yearly rate. At 8% it takes about 9 years; at 2%, about 36.
By the Rule of 72, a balance growing at about 22% a year would double in a little over 3 years if nothing were paid.

title: Franklin's compound-interest bequest
description: Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia to be lent at 5% for 200 years, calculating that compounding would make it £131,000 in a century.

facts.text: In a 1789 codicil to his will, Benjamin Franklin left £1,000 each to Boston and Philadelphia, to be lent at 5% interest to young tradesmen in a plan lasting 200 years.
Franklin calculated that after 100 years at 5%, Boston's £1,000 would have grown to £131,000.
At 5% simple interest, £1,000 earns £50 a year, or £5,000 over 100 years: £6,000 in all, about £125,000 less than Franklin's compounded £131,000.
The funds were badly managed and fell short of Franklin's estimates, but by 1990 Boston's had grown to about $4.5 million.

title: How a credit card borrows
description: A credit card is revolving credit: you borrow up to a limit, and a balance paid in full by the due date may avoid interest on purchases.

facts.text: Revolving credit, most of which is credit card lending, lets a consumer borrow up to a set limit and repay in one or more installments.
If you pay a credit card balance in full by the due date, you may not be charged interest on purchases; any unpaid portion is charged interest.

title: Credit card interest and minimum payments
description: Card interest rates are high and compounding makes unpaid balances grow; US statements must warn about paying only the minimum.

facts.text: In 2026, US credit card accounts that were charged interest paid an average rate of about 22% a year.
US card statements must carry a Minimum Payment Warning: paying only the minimum means paying more interest and taking longer to pay off the balance.
Card statements must also estimate how long paying only the minimum would take to clear the balance, and the total it would cost.

title: What a credit score is
description: A credit score predicts how likely you are to repay on time, based on your credit reports; higher scores usually mean easier approval and better rates.

facts.text: A credit score is a prediction of your credit behavior, such as how likely you are to pay a loan back on time, based on your credit reports.
Most credit scores fall between 300 and 850.
Usually a higher credit score makes it easier to qualify for a loan and may bring a better interest rate or loan terms.

title: What goes into a credit score
description: A FICO score weighs payment history, amounts owed, length of history, new credit and credit mix; income isn't in it, and nobody has just one score.

facts.text: FICO scores weigh five categories: payment history 35%, amounts owed 30%, length of credit history 15%, new credit 10% and credit mix 10%.
A FICO score is calculated only from the information in your credit report, so income isn't part of it, though lenders may look at income separately.
You don't have just one credit score: scores vary with the scoring model, the data used and even the day they're calculated.

title: A mortgage: a loan pledged on a home
description: A mortgage lets the lender take the property if the loan isn't repaid; the word means 'dead pledge' because the pledge ends either way.

facts.text: Mortgage comes from Old French mort gage, 'dead pledge': the pledge dies either when the debt is paid or when payment fails and the land is lost.
A mortgage is an agreement that gives the lender the right to take your property if you don't repay the money borrowed plus interest.

title: Why mortgages last decades
description: Longer mortgages mean lower monthly payments but more total cost; early payments are mostly interest (amortization).

facts.text: Compared with a 15-year mortgage, a 30-year mortgage usually has lower monthly payments but a higher interest rate and a higher total cost.
Early in a mortgage most of each payment goes to interest because the balance is high; over time more goes to paying off the loan. This is amortization.
The equity you build in a home is much less than the sum of your mortgage payments, because the interest doesn't reduce your balance.

title: Secured and unsecured loans
description: Secured loans are backed by collateral and usually cost less; unsecured loans have none, so lenders see more risk and may charge more.

facts.text: A secured loan is backed by collateral, such as a car or home, which the lender can take and sell to get its money back if the loan isn't repaid.
Secured loans are less risky to lenders, so they usually have lower interest rates and higher borrowing limits.
An unsecured loan uses no property as collateral; lenders see it as riskier, so they may charge a higher interest rate.
Lenders may grant unsecured loans based on a borrower's income and credit record.
Car loans are typically secured by the car, while student loans, personal loans and credit cards are typically unsecured.

title: Microcredit and Grameen Bank
description: Muhammad Yunus showed that small loans without collateral could work for the poor, founding Grameen Bank and sharing the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize.

facts.text: In 1976, economist Muhammad Yunus began lending to the poor in Bangladesh, starting with $27 of his own money lent to 42 women in the village of Jobra.
By 1983 the project had become Grameen Bank, which makes small loans to poor people who have no collateral.
In 2006, Muhammad Yunus and Grameen Bank shared the Nobel Peace Prize.

title: Bank runs
description: Banks cannot pay all depositors at once, so a rush to withdraw can sink a bank, and fear of a run makes joining it rational.

facts.text: On March 9, 2023, customers withdrew more than $40 billion from Silicon Valley Bank; regulators seized the bank the next day.
Banks borrow short term (deposits can be withdrawn) and lend for long periods, which is called maturity transformation.
Banks keep funds in reserve for depositors who want their money out, but can't pay off all their depositors at once.
A bank run is an attempt by many depositors to withdraw their money at the same time, and it can put a bank out of business.
Once many depositors rush to withdraw, the bank really is at risk, so it makes sense for other depositors to withdraw too.
Economists Douglas Diamond and Philip Dybvig formalized how bank runs can feed themselves, work recognized in the 2022 Nobel Prize in economics.

title: Deposit insurance
description: US deposit insurance (the FDIC, since 1933) guarantees deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category, to keep public confidence.

facts.text: The FDIC was created by the Banking Act of 1933, after thousands of bank failures in the 1920s and early 1930s.
FDIC deposit insurance covers $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, for each account ownership category.
Since the FDIC was founded in 1933, no depositor has lost a penny of FDIC-insured funds.
The FDIC was created to maintain stability and public confidence in the nation's financial system.

title: Credit means trust
description: The word credit comes from Latin credere, 'to trust, entrust, believe': lending and borrowing run on trust.

facts.text: Credit comes from Latin creditum, 'a loan, thing entrusted to another', from credere, 'to trust, entrust, believe'.

title: Emergency funds
description: An emergency fund is cash set aside for unplanned costs, kept somewhere safe and easy to reach. In 2024, 63% of US adults said they could cover a $400 surprise with cash or its equivalent.

facts.text: In the Federal Reserve's survey for 2024, 63% of US adults said they would cover a $400 emergency expense using only cash or its equivalent.
In the same 2024 survey, 13% of US adults said they could not pay a $400 emergency expense by any means.
An emergency fund is cash set aside for unplanned expenses, such as car repairs, medical bills, a broken phone or a loss of income.
An emergency fund should be kept somewhere safe and accessible, such as a bank account, where you are not tempted to spend it on non-emergencies.

title: Saving for goals, and the price of safety
description: Saving toward a specific goal helps people stay motivated. Savings kept safe and reachable usually earn a low interest rate: the tradeoff between security and availability.

facts.text: Having a specific goal for your savings can help you stay motivated.
Savings are usually kept in safe places you can reach at any time, like savings accounts, but there is a tradeoff between security and availability: the money earns a low interest rate.

title: The risk-return tradeoff
description: In finance, risk is uncertainty about what an investment will return. As risk rises, investors seek higher returns to compensate, and people with longer time horizons can more easily ride out risky investments.

facts.text: In finance, risk is the uncertainty about what an investment will return, including the chance of losing money.
In general, as investment risks rise, investors seek higher returns to compensate themselves for taking those risks.
Investors with a longer time horizon may be comfortable with riskier, more volatile investments; those with a shorter horizon may prefer less risky ones.
Past performance is actual historical information, but it cannot predict how an investment will perform in the future.

title: Stocks and Treasury bills since 1928
description: From 1928 to 2025, US stocks grew far more than Treasury bills but had big losing years, while bills never lost money in a year.

facts.text: From the start of 1928 to the end of 2025, $100 in US large-company stocks (the S&P 500, dividends reinvested) grew to over $1 million, while $100 in 3-month US Treasury bills grew to about $2,600, before inflation.
US stocks' worst year from 1928 to 2025 was 1931, when they lost more than 40%; they lost money in 26 of those 98 years.
3-month US Treasury bills did not have a single losing calendar year from 1928 to 2025.

title: What a share of stock is
description: A stock is a share of ownership in a company. Companies sell shares to raise money; shareholders can gain from dividends and rising prices, and common shareholders usually vote, but prices can fall.

facts.text: A stock gives its holder a share of ownership in a company.
Companies issue stock to raise money for things like paying off debt, launching products, expanding or building facilities.
Common stock usually entitles its owners to vote at shareholder meetings.
Shareholders can gain from dividends, when a company distributes some of its earnings, and from capital appreciation, when the stock rises in price.
Stock prices move down as well as up, and there is no guarantee a company will do well, so you can lose money invested in stocks.

title: The VOC and the first public shares
description: In 1602 the Dutch East India Company (VOC) let the public buy its shares, making it the first publicly traded company. Shares changed hands in a register, and the first dividend (1610) was paid in mace.

facts.text: In 1602, the Dutch East India Company (VOC) let members of the public buy its shares; it is considered the first publicly traded company.
1,143 investors subscribed to the VOC in Amsterdam in 1602.
VOC shares could be transferred to a new owner through the company bookkeeper, who recorded the transfer in a register.
The VOC's first dividend was paid in 1610 in mace, a spice, worth 75% of the share capital.

title: How a bond works
description: A bond is an IOU: you lend to a government, city or company, which pays interest on a schedule and repays the face value at maturity.

facts.text: A bond is a debt security, like an IOU: buying one means lending to the issuer, which may be a government, a municipality or a corporation.
A bond issuer promises to pay a specified rate of interest, typically on a schedule such as every six months, and to repay the face value when the bond matures.

title: Bond risks and who gets paid first
description: Bonds can default, and a bond sold early may fetch less if interest rates have risen. If a company goes bankrupt, bondholders are paid before shareholders.

facts.text: Bonds can provide a predictable income stream and can help offset more volatile stock holdings.
A bond issuer may fail to make interest or principal payments on time, which is a default.
If a company goes bankrupt and its assets are sold, bondholders are paid before stockholders; common stockholders get whatever is left, which may be nothing.
When interest rates rise, new bonds pay more than older ones, so an older bond sold before maturity may have to be sold at a discount.

title: Britain's War Loan
description: Britain's 3.5% War Loan traced back to borrowing in 1917 for World War I. It had no fixed maturity, so the government chose when to repay: in 2015, when rates were low.

facts.text: Britain's 3½% War Loan traced back to the 5% War Loan, issued in 1917 to raise money for World War I.
On 9 March 2015, the UK government repaid the £1.9 billion of 3½% War Loan still outstanding, then held by more than 120,000 holders.
In 1932, 5% War Loan holders were persuaded to switch to the lower-paying 3½% War Loan, which had no fixed maturity date.
The UK repaid the 3½% War Loan in 2015 while interest rates were exceptionally low.

title: Stock exchanges as meeting places
description: The NYSE traces its origins to the Buttonwood Agreement of 1792. An exchange gathers buyers and sellers so investors can nearly always buy or sell.

facts.text: The New York Stock Exchange traces its origins to the Buttonwood Agreement, signed by 24 stockbrokers on May 17, 1792.
The Buttonwood brokers, meeting under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street, signed a two-sentence agreement to trade with each other at fixed commissions.
Stock exchanges bring buyers and sellers together and guarantee a basic level of liquidity, so investors are always able to buy or sell their stocks.

title: Bids, asks and orders
description: The bid is the highest price a buyer will pay, the ask the lowest a seller will take, and the gap is the spread. Orders are matched automatically; a market order trades now, a limit order only at your price or better.

facts.text: A stock's bid is the highest price a buyer will pay and its ask is the lowest price a seller will accept; the ask is almost always higher, and the difference is the spread.
Electronic trading networks automatically match buy and sell orders at specified prices.
A stock's last-traded price is not necessarily the price at which a new market order will be executed.
A market order buys or sells immediately; it is guaranteed to execute, but the price is not guaranteed.
A limit order executes only at a set price or better: a buy limit at that price or lower, a sell limit at that price or higher.

title: Diversification
description: Diversification means spreading money among different investments, across and within asset classes, to reduce risk. Funds make it easy, but it can't prevent losses in a market-wide drop.

facts.text: Diversification is spreading money among different investments to reduce risk, summed up as "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
You can diversify across asset classes, such as stocks, bonds and cash, and within them, by holding many different stocks or bonds in different industries.
The idea of diversification is that if one investment or sector does poorly, others doing well may offset the loss.
Diversification can't guarantee your investments won't suffer if the market drops, but it can improve the chances that you won't lose money, or won't lose as much.
Mutual funds and ETFs pool money from many investors and invest it in stocks, bonds and other assets, so each investor owns a small portion of many investments.
A fund narrowly focused on one industry sector will not necessarily provide diversification.

title: Enron's one-basket 401(k)
description: At the end of 2000, most of Enron's 401(k) plan assets were in Enron stock. When Enron went bankrupt in December 2001, many employees lost their jobs and much of their retirement savings.

facts.text: At the end of 2000, more than half of the money in Enron's 401(k) retirement plan was invested in Enron's own stock.
Enron went bankrupt on December 2, 2001, and many of its employees lost both their jobs and much of their 401(k) retirement savings.

title: How index funds work
description: An index fund tracks a market index such as the S&P 500 by holding all or a sample of its securities. It trades rarely, can cost less to run, and carries the same risks as its index.

facts.text: A market index, such as the S&P 500, measures the performance of a basket of securities; you cannot invest in an index directly.
An index fund is a mutual fund or ETF that seeks to track the returns of a market index, holding all or a sample of the securities in it.
Index funds generally invest passively, buying and selling rarely, while actively managed funds trade more often to try to outperform an index.
Because index fund managers do not pay research analysts to pick securities, index funds may cost less to run, though not every index fund is cheaper.
Fees reduce your return: if two funds hold investments that perform identically, the lower-cost fund generally returns more.
An index fund is subject to the same general risks as the securities in the index it tracks.

title: Index funds: from 'Bogle's Folly' to the majority
description: John Bogle's First Index Investment Trust (1976) raised about $11 million and was mocked as 'Bogle's Folly'. Most active large-cap funds have trailed the S&P 500 over 15 years, and US index-style funds overtook active funds in assets at the end of 2023.

facts.text: John Bogle launched First Index Investment Trust, tracking the S&P 500, on August 31, 1976; it was the first index fund for individual investors.
Bogle hoped to raise up to $150 million for the first index fund, but it raised only about $11 million.
Critics called the first index fund a path to mediocrity, and some nicknamed it 'Bogle's Folly'.
Over the 15 years to the end of 2024, 89.5% of actively managed US large-company stock funds did worse than the S&P 500.
At the end of 2023, passive (index-tracking) mutual funds and ETFs in the US held more assets than actively managed funds for the first time.

title: Starting early: time does the work
description: The earlier you start saving, the more time money has to grow. In the SEC's example, $365 saved once at 5% a year becomes $465.84 after five years and $1,577.50 after 30.

facts.text: In an SEC example, a $1 candy bar every day costs $365 a year; saved and earning 5% a year, that $365 grows to $465.84 in five years and $1,577.50 in 30 years.
In the SEC candy-bar example, the $365 gains about $101 in its first five years and about $1,112 in the following 25 years (derived from $465.84 and $1,577.50).
Starting early is key to saving enough for retirement: the younger you are when you begin, the more time your investments have to grow.

title: Pensions and 401(k)-style plans
description: A traditional pension pays a set benefit the employer funds and invests. In a 401(k)-style plan the worker chooses how much to save and how to invest it, sometimes with an employer match, and carries the investment risk.

facts.text: In a traditional defined benefit pension, the employer contributes and invests the money and pays retirees a benefit based on their pay and years of service.
In a defined contribution plan such as a 401(k), the worker chooses how much to contribute from each paycheck and where the money is invested.
Some employers add a matching contribution to a worker's retirement plan, for instance 50 cents for every dollar the worker saves.
As retirement savings moved from traditional pensions to 401(k)s, investment risk shifted from employers to employees.

title: Income and price: where returns come from
description: An investment can pay through income, such as dividends, interest or rent, and through a change in its price. Total return is the income plus the price gain or minus the price loss.

facts.text: An investment is an asset acquired to make a financial gain through income or an increase in value.
An investment's total return is the income it pays, such as dividends, plus its gain in price (or minus its loss).

title: Property as an investment
description: Real estate can pay through rent and through changes in its value. REITs own income-producing property and let investors share its income; non-traded REITs are hard to sell.

facts.text: Real estate can produce income, such as rent, and its value can rise or fall.
A REIT is a company that owns and typically operates income-producing real estate, such as offices, apartments and warehouses, letting investors share its income without buying property.
Some REITs trade on stock exchanges; non-traded REITs are illiquid and generally cannot be sold readily.

title: Commodities, futures and gold
description: Commodities such as metals, grains and oil trade mostly through futures contracts, a practice pioneered at Osaka's Dojima rice market (1730). Gold pays no income, and precious metals are highly volatile.

facts.text: In Edo-period Japan, feudal domains sold rice collected as tax to brokers in exchange for rice bills, notes exchangeable for rice, which were actively traded.
In 1730, Japan's Tokugawa shogunate authorized the Dojima Rice Exchange in Osaka, with a futures market in rice; it is widely seen as the forerunner of organized futures exchanges.
A commodity futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell a set quantity of a commodity at a set price on a future date; metals, grains and other foods trade this way.
Gold pays no dividends or interest, so its return depends on someone paying more for it later.
US regulators warn that gold and other precious metals are highly volatile and that past performance is not a good predictor of future returns.

title: Comparing homes for money: safety, growth and access
description: Every saving and investment product differs in how safe the money is, how fast it can grow and how readily you can get it back. A liquid asset can be turned into cash quickly.

facts.text: Every saving and investment product has different risks and returns, including how readily you can get your money, how fast it will grow and how safe it will be.
A liquid asset is one that can be readily converted into cash within a short time.
From the start of 1928 to the end of 2025, before inflation, $100 grew to about $2,600 in 3-month Treasury bills, about $7,750 in 10-year US Treasury bonds and over $1 million in US stocks.

title: What a market is
description: A market is any way buyers and sellers get in contact to exchange goods and services, directly or through go-betweens. It need not be a place.

facts.text: A market is any means by which buyers and sellers get in contact to exchange goods and services, either directly or through go-betweens.
In modern economies, a market is not a single place: it covers the whole area in which sellers compete for customers.

title: eBay's first sale
description: In 1995, the first item sold on AuctionWeb, the site that became eBay, was a broken laser pointer, for $14.83.

facts.text: Pierre Omidyar launched AuctionWeb, the site that became eBay, over Labor Day weekend in 1995.
The first item sold on AuctionWeb was a broken laser pointer, which sold for $14.83.

title: Markets for work and savings
description: Supply and demand apply to any market: goods and services, labor and financial capital.

facts.text: Supply and demand apply to any market, including labor markets, where job seekers supply work and employers demand it, and financial markets, where savers supply funds and borrowers demand them.
Along with the growth of trade in goods, financial markets such as securities exchanges have multiplied.
In financial markets, savers expect to receive a rate of return and borrowers expect to pay one; the simplest example is the interest rate.

title: The law of supply
description: When a price rises, sellers offer more; when it falls, they offer less, because higher prices mean more profit.

facts.text: Law of supply: a rise in price almost always increases the quantity supplied, and a fall in price decreases it.
Higher prices encourage profit-seeking firms to expand production and bring more of the product to market.
A supply curve, drawn with price on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal, usually slopes upward.

title: What shifts supply
description: Supply and demand curves assume other things stay equal (ceteris paribus). Costs, weather, technology and government policy shift the whole supply curve; a price change only moves along it.

facts.text: Supply and demand curves assume all other things stay the same, which economists call ceteris paribus, 'other things being equal'.
Supply shifts with the costs of production: input prices, natural conditions such as weather, technology, and government taxes, regulations and subsidies.
A change in a good's own price moves buyers or sellers along its demand or supply curve; other factors shift the whole curve.

title: The law of demand
description: When a price rises, buyers want less; when it falls, they want more. The demand curve slopes downward.

facts.text: Law of demand: a rise in price almost always decreases the quantity demanded, and a fall in price increases it.
A demand curve almost always slopes downward: consumers buy more at lower prices.
When gasoline prices rise, people cut back by combining errands, carpooling or taking mass transit, and taking trips closer to home.

title: Why buyers want less at higher prices
description: The substitution effect (switching to relatively cheaper goods) and the income effect (a higher price shrinks buying power) both cut the quantity demanded.

facts.text: Substitution effect: when a price changes, consumers buy less of the good that is now relatively pricier and more of the one that is relatively cheaper.
Income effect: a higher price reduces the buying power of income, even though income hasn't changed, so people buy less of a normal good.

title: What shifts demand
description: Income, tastes, prices of related goods, population and expectations shift the whole demand curve.

facts.text: Demand shifts with income, tastes, the prices of related goods (substitutes and complements), population and expectations about the future.

title: Equilibrium price
description: The price where supply and demand cross: quantity demanded equals quantity supplied.

facts.text: The equilibrium price is the only price where the quantity buyers want to buy equals the quantity sellers want to sell.
In markets, the interplay of supply and demand determines prices.

title: How surpluses and shortages move prices
description: Above equilibrium there is a surplus and sellers cut prices; below it there is a shortage and sellers raise prices.

facts.text: Above the equilibrium price, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded: a surplus, or excess supply.
Below the equilibrium price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied: a shortage, or excess demand.
In a surplus, some sellers cut prices, because selling at a lower price is better than not selling at all.
In a shortage, sellers see a chance to earn more by charging a higher price.

title: Marshall's scissors
description: Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: price comes from both together.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall's most important work was Principles of Economics, published in 1890.
Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: disputing which one sets value is like disputing which blade does the cutting.

title: Price floors cause surpluses
description: A price floor is a legal minimum price. Set above equilibrium, it creates a surplus.

facts.text: Price controls are laws governments use to regulate prices; they come as price ceilings and price floors.
A price floor is the lowest price one can legally pay for a good or service.
A price floor set above the equilibrium price creates a surplus: quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded.

title: Price ceilings cause shortages
description: A price ceiling is a legal maximum price. Set below equilibrium, it creates a shortage, as with rent control.

facts.text: A price ceiling is the highest price one can legally pay for a good or service, often set to keep necessities affordable.
A price ceiling set below the equilibrium price creates a shortage: quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Rent control can leave fewer apartments available to rent than there would be at market rates.

title: Europe's butter mountains
description: The EU's Common Agricultural Policy held farm prices artificially high, farmers produced more, and by the 1980s huge surpluses of butter and wine piled up.

facts.text: When it was created in 1962, the EU's Common Agricultural Policy supported farmers mainly by keeping their prices artificially high.
The artificially high prices encouraged farmers to produce more and more.
In the 1980s, this led to huge stored surpluses of butter and wine, known as butter mountains and wine lakes; the 'wine' was actually industrial alcohol.

title: Price takers
description: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products, so each must accept the market price.

facts.text: In perfect competition, many firms sell identical products to many buyers, everyone has the relevant information, and firms can enter and leave freely.
A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: competition forces it to accept the market price, which supply and demand across the whole market set.
A farmer who tried to sell corn above the market price would find no buyers.

title: Profits attract rivals
description: Profits draw new firms into a market; their extra supply pushes the price down until profits are squeezed away.

facts.text: In a competitive market, profits attract new firms; their entry eventually brings the price down until economic profits are driven to zero and no more firms want to enter.

title: What competition does for buyers
description: Competition pushes businesses to operate efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up, and brings more choice and innovation.

facts.text: Protecting competition gives businesses strong incentives to operate efficiently, keep prices down and keep quality up.
Competition brings consumers lower prices, higher quality products and services, more choices and greater innovation.

title: What a monopoly is
description: A monopoly is a single supplier of something with no substitute, protected by barriers to entry.

facts.text: A monopoly is the exclusive possession of a market by a supplier of a product or service for which there is no substitute.
A monopolist can set its price without fear of competition from other sellers or substitute products.
Barriers to entry are the legal, technological or market forces that discourage or prevent competitors from entering a market.
With high barriers to entry, big profits need not attract new firms or bring the price down.
The board game Monopoly grew out of The Landlord's Game, which Lizzie Magie patented in 1904 to teach economic ideas about land and rent.

title: Why monopolies hurt buyers
description: A monopoly sells less at a higher price than a competitive market, and faces less pressure to improve.

facts.text: A monopoly sells a lower quantity at a higher price than a perfectly competitive market would, so consumers do not benefit.
With no competition to fear, a monopoly can keep making the same old products in the same old way; in 1935 John Hicks wrote, 'The best of all monopoly profits is a quiet life.'

title: Standard Oil and antitrust
description: Standard Oil dominated US refining until the Supreme Court broke it up in 1911 under the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890.

facts.text: By 1880, Standard Oil controlled the refining of 90 to 95 percent of the oil produced in the United States.
The Sherman Act, passed in 1890, outlaws monopolization and attempts to monopolize a market.
In 1911, the US Supreme Court ordered Standard Oil to be broken up into separate companies.

title: Incentives
description: Incentives are rewards (positive) and penalties (negative) that encourage or discourage choices; people respond to them in predictable ways. Prices are incentives too.

facts.text: Positive incentives are rewards that encourage a behavior; negative incentives are penalties that discourage one.
Speeding tickets and littering fines are incentives set by governments; buy-one-get-one-free sales are incentives set by businesses.
People respond to incentives, and incentives are usually meant to make people behave in predictable ways.
Economic incentives involve a financial benefit or cost, so they can be positive or negative.

title: Hanoi's rat bounty
description: In colonial Hanoi, a bounty paid per rat tail led people to cut off tails, release rats to breed, and farm rats.

facts.text: In colonial Hanoi in 1902, the French authorities paid a few cents for each rat tail delivered to the police.
People cut the tails off rats and let them go free to breed more rats.
Officials found people farming rats, and a network smuggling rats into the city.

title: Scarcity, the basic problem of economics
description: Scarcity means people's wants exceed what's available, for everyone; time is the ultimate scarce resource. Economics studies how people choose under scarcity.

facts.text: Scarcity means that human wants for goods, services and resources exceed what is available.
Time is the ultimate scarce resource: everyone, rich or poor, has the same 24 hours in a day.
Economics is the study of how humans make decisions in the face of scarcity.
In 1932, Lionel Robbins defined economics as the science of human behavior as a relationship between ends and scarce means which have alternative uses.

title: The water and diamond puzzle
description: Water is vital but cheap, diamonds are nearly useless but dear. The standard explanation is scarcity: water is plentiful, diamonds are not.

facts.text: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith noted that nothing is more useful than water, yet it buys scarcely anything, while a diamond has scarcely any use yet trades for a great quantity of other goods.
The standard explanation: water is plentiful, so one more unit is worth little to people; diamonds are scarce, so each one is worth a lot.

title: Prices carry information
description: Hayek (1945): the price system communicates information. When something becomes scarcer, its price tells users to economize without their needing to know why.

facts.text: In 1945, Friedrich Hayek imagined tin becoming scarcer, from a new use or a lost source; tin users need not know which, only that they must economize on tin.
Hayek described the price system as a mechanism for communicating information, which gets tens of thousands of people to use a material more sparingly without anyone directing them.

title: What taxes pay for
description: Governments collect taxes to pay for what they provide: in the US, federal money goes mostly to defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest; states and cities spend most on education.

facts.text: In a 1789 letter, Benjamin Franklin wrote that in this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes.
Governments collect taxes to pay for the public services and programs they provide.
The biggest items of US federal spending are national defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest payments on past borrowing.
The biggest item for US state and local governments is education; they also pay for highways, libraries, parks and police and fire protection.
In 2023, taxes averaged 33.9% of GDP across OECD countries, ranging from under a fifth in Mexico to over two-fifths in France and Denmark.

title: The main kinds of tax
description: Taxes fall on what people earn (income, payroll and corporate taxes), what they buy (sales taxes, VATs and excise taxes) and what they own (property and estate taxes).

facts.text: Taxes are classified by what they fall on: income and profits, payroll, property, and goods and services.
US federal taxes include individual income tax, payroll taxes on wages, corporate income tax on profits, excise taxes on goods like gasoline, tobacco and alcohol, and estate taxes.
US state and local governments rely heavily on sales taxes and property taxes.
A value-added tax (VAT) is collected at each stage of production: each business pays tax on its sales and gets credit for the tax already paid on its inputs.
More than 170 countries use a VAT; the United States is the only OECD country without one and relies on state and local sales taxes instead.

title: Progressive, proportional and regressive taxes
description: A progressive tax takes a higher share of higher incomes, a proportional (flat) tax the same share from everyone, a regressive tax a smaller share of higher incomes. Flat taxes have supporters and critics.

facts.text: A progressive tax takes a higher share of income from people with higher incomes; the US federal income tax is an example.
A proportional, or flat, tax takes the same share of income from everyone; the US Medicare payroll tax is an example.
A regressive tax takes a smaller share of income from people with higher incomes.
In 1994, Estonia became the first country in Eastern Europe to introduce a flat personal income tax.
Sales taxes tend to be regressive because lower-income households spend a larger share of their income on goods than higher-income households do.
Supporters of a flat income tax argue it is simpler, removes deductions that special interests exploit, and encourages people to work, save and invest.
Critics of a flat income tax argue it is unfair, shifting the burden toward lower- and middle-income households, and could reduce government revenue.

title: Tax brackets and marginal rates
description: In a bracketed income tax, only the income inside a higher bracket is taxed at that bracket's rate, so a raise never lowers take-home pay.

facts.text: In a bracketed income tax, only the income that falls inside a higher bracket is taxed at that higher rate, not your whole income.
Because only the extra dollars are taxed at the higher rate, moving into a higher bracket never lowers your take-home pay.

title: Public goods
description: A public good is nonexcludable and nonrival, like national defense; because non-payers cannot be kept out, governments usually fund such goods through taxes.

facts.text: A public good is nonexcludable (it is costly or impossible to stop people using it) and nonrival (one person using it does not stop others using it).
National defense is a classic public good: it protects everyone in a country at once, and no one can be left out of it.
When people agree through the political process to pay taxes for a public good, they can overcome the free rider problem.

title: The free rider problem
description: When non-payers cannot be excluded, each person has an incentive to let others pay and enjoy the good for free, so a good everyone values may never be produced.

facts.text: With a fireworks show, each person may try to free ride: let others pay for the show, then watch it for free from their own backyard.
Free riding means letting others pay for a good and enjoying it without paying yourself.
If free riding cannot be solved, goods that people would be willing to pay for may never be produced.

title: The lighthouse debate
description: Economists long used the lighthouse as a public good; Ronald Coase showed in 1974 that English lighthouses were privately run and paid for by light dues collected at ports, though critics note the dues were backed by the Crown.

facts.text: Economists from John Stuart Mill to Paul Samuelson used the lighthouse as an example of something private firms could not easily provide, because ships could not be made to pay.
In 1974, economist Ronald Coase showed that many of England's early lighthouses were privately built and run, paid for by light dues collected from ships at ports.
Critics of Coase point out that the right to collect light dues came from a royal patent, so government still enforced payment.

title: Budget deficits and surpluses
description: A government runs a deficit in a year when it spends more than it collects, a surplus when it collects more than it spends, and a balanced budget when the two are equal.

facts.text: A government runs a budget deficit in a year when it spends more than it collects in taxes.
A government runs a budget surplus when it collects more than it spends, and has a balanced budget when the two are equal.
The US federal government last ran a budget surplus in 2001.

title: The national debt
description: The national debt is the sum of past deficits and surpluses: governments cover deficits by selling bonds, and the debt is that borrowing plus interest. Economists weigh its costs and uses differently.

facts.text: In 2015, the UK government repaid old undated bonds that included debts from the South Sea Bubble of 1720 and borrowing used to fund the Napoleonic Wars.
To pay for a deficit, a government borrows, largely by selling bonds; the national debt is all that borrowing added up, plus interest owed.
A deficit is one year's gap; the debt is the running total. Borrow $10,000 a year for four years and your yearly deficit is $10,000, but your debt is $40,000.
Some economists worry that heavy government borrowing soaks up savings and leaves less for private investment, which they call crowding out.
Others point out that government spending on roads, water systems, education and research can encourage long-term growth.

title: What a central bank does
description: A central bank runs monetary policy, watches over banks and keeps payments safe. Sweden's Riksbank (1668) is the oldest; the US Federal Reserve dates from 1913 and aims for maximum employment and stable prices.

facts.text: Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668 from the ruins of the failed Stockholms Banco, is the world's oldest central bank.
Johan Palmstruch, founder of Stockholms Banco, was found guilty of mismanaging it and sentenced to death, then reprieved.
The US central bank, the Federal Reserve, was created in 1913; its jobs include conducting monetary policy, supervising banks, promoting financial stability and keeping payments safe.
From 1668, the Riksbank's law told it to keep the country's coinage at its 'right and fair value', an early price-stability goal.
Since 1977, Congress has told the Federal Reserve to pursue maximum employment and stable prices, often called its dual mandate.

title: Central bank independence
description: Central banks are kept at arm's length from elected politicians so short-term election pressures do not push up inflation; critics question how much power unelected officials should hold.

facts.text: Governments may be tempted to stimulate the economy, for example before elections, even at the cost of higher inflation.
Federal Reserve governors serve staggered 14-year terms, and elected officials are not allowed to serve on its Board.
A study of 155 central banks over 50 years found that greater independence helped keep inflation in check.
Critics question whether unelected central bankers should hold so much power; Paul Tucker, a former Bank of England deputy governor, explored this in his 2018 book Unelected Power.
The Federal Reserve answers to Congress: its chair testifies and it reports on monetary policy twice a year.

title: How a central bank's rate moves the economy
description: A central bank sets a core short-term rate that feeds into loan and savings rates; raising it cools spending and price rises, cutting it encourages borrowing, spending and hiring, with long and variable lags.

facts.text: A central bank sets a core short-term interest rate, like the Bank of England's Bank Rate, which influences the rates banks charge on loans and pay on savings.
When a central bank raises rates, loan and mortgage payments rise and saving pays more, so people spend less and businesses find it harder to raise prices.
When a central bank cuts rates, borrowing gets cheaper, so households and businesses spend more and businesses hire more workers.
In 1959, economist Milton Friedman told Congress that monetary policy works with a long and variable lag; in his study the delay ranged from 4 to 29 months.

title: The Volcker rate hikes
description: Under Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let its key rate approach 20% in 1980 and 1981 to fight high inflation; inflation fell to 5% by late 1982, but a deep recession pushed unemployment near 11%.

facts.text: Under chair Paul Volcker, the Federal Reserve let its key interest rate, the federal funds rate, approach 20% in late 1980 and early 1981 to fight high inflation.
The high rates hit borrowing-dependent industries like construction and autos, and US unemployment reached nearly 11% late in 1982.
By October 1982, US inflation had fallen to 5%.

title: Money growth and prices
description: If the amount of money grows faster than the goods and services it buys, prices rise; the link is real over long periods but not mechanical, because how fast money changes hands can shift.

facts.text: In Radford's camp, big deliveries of several hundred thousand cigarettes could arrive within a fortnight; prices soared, then fell as stocks ran out.
The quantity theory of money says that when money grows faster than the output of goods and services, the extra money pushes up prices rather than output.
Milton Friedman proposed that money should grow at the same rate as the economy: if output grows 2% a year, money should grow 2%, leaving prices unchanged.
The link is not mechanical: in the 1980s and 1990s, how fast money changed hands became unstable, and many economists dropped strict money-growth rules.
Most economists now agree that prices cannot keep rising indefinitely without the money supply growing.

title: The price revolution
description: In the 16th century, silver from American mines like Potosí flowed into Spain and across Europe while prices rose about sixfold; historians also point to population growth.

facts.text: From 1550 onward, silver from American mines, chiefly Potosí, arrived in Spain in huge volumes and spread across Europe.
During the 16th-century price revolution, European prices rose about sixfold.
Historians also link the price revolution to a growing population needing food and housing, and still debate how much each cause mattered.

title: Rules for when sellers know more
description: When one side of a deal knows more about quality (asymmetric information), rules like food-safety and truth-in-advertising laws help buyers; The Jungle led to two such laws in 1906.

facts.text: Upton Sinclair's 1906 novel The Jungle showed filthy conditions in Chicago's meatpacking plants and helped push food-safety laws through Congress.
On June 30, 1906, President Theodore Roosevelt signed both the Meat Inspection Act and the Pure Food and Drug Act.
Asymmetric information is when one side of a deal, buyer or seller, knows more about the product's quality than the other.
The 1906 food law banned adulterated and misbranded food and drugs from being shipped between states.
US advertising rules allow exaggeration, but a claim presented as a fact must be true.
Occupational licenses reassure customers that a worker is trained, but they can also be a barrier to entering an industry.

title: Capital rules for banks
description: Regulators make banks fund part of their lending with owners' money (capital), a cushion that absorbs losses before depositors are hurt; higher requirements make banks safer but may slow lending.

facts.text: Regulators require banks to hold capital: owners' money that acts as a cushion, so a bank can absorb big losses without failing to repay its depositors.
Capital rules aim to make bank failures and government bailouts less likely.
Higher capital requirements make banks safer but may slow growth by limiting how much banks lend.

title: The first social insurance
description: Germany under Otto von Bismarck created the first old-age social insurance in 1889, paid for by workers, employers and the government, with benefits from age 70.

facts.text: In 1889, Germany, under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck, became the first nation to adopt old-age social insurance.
Germany's 1889 old-age insurance gave workers basic security from age 70.
Workers, employers and the government all paid into Germany's system.

title: Unemployment insurance
description: Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose jobs through no fault of their own; economists weigh its support for families against effects on job search.

facts.text: Unemployment insurance gives temporary, partial wage replacement to workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own.
Unemployment benefits help people who lost a job keep paying their bills while they look for work.
Studies find that longer benefits can lengthen unemployment somewhat, yet people receiving benefits search hard for work.

title: Pay-as-you-go pensions
description: US Social Security is pay-as-you-go: today's workers' taxes fund today's beneficiaries, so fewer workers per retiree (about four in 1965, 2.7 in 2023) strains the system.

facts.text: US Social Security is pay-as-you-go: taxes paid by today's workers fund payments to today's beneficiaries, rather than filling personal accounts.
In 1965, there were about four workers paying into US Social Security for each beneficiary; by 2023, there were 2.7.
Pay-as-you-go pension systems come under strain as the number of retirees grows relative to the workers paying in.

title: Fiscal policy and monetary policy
description: Fiscal policy is government spending and taxing, set in the US by Congress and the administration; monetary policy is what the central bank does with interest rates and money.

facts.text: Fiscal policy means government spending and taxing decisions; in the US, Congress and the administration make them.
Monetary policy means the actions a central bank takes, mainly on interest rates, to pursue goals like stable prices and maximum employment.
