The Federal Reserve plays no role in setting taxes or government spending.

title: What inflation is
description: Inflation is the rate at which prices rise across an economy over time; it lowers the purchasing power of money.

facts.text: In Radford's camp, several hundred thousand cigarettes might arrive in a fortnight; prices soared, then fell as stocks ran out.
Inflation is the rate at which prices rise over a period of time; it is a broad measure of the overall increase in prices in a country.
Inflation lowers purchasing power: each unit of money buys less, and people whose income rises more slowly than prices can afford less.

title: Why prices rise, and the debate
description: Demand-pull, cost-push and expectations drive inflation; economists disagree about how much the money supply matters.

facts.text: Demand-pull inflation happens when overall demand grows faster than an economy can produce: 'too much money chasing too few goods'.
Cost-push inflation happens when a supply shock, such as higher oil prices, raises production costs or disrupts supply.
If people and firms expect higher prices, they build those expectations into wage deals and contract prices.
Economists disagree on inflation's causes: monetarists stress money supply growth; Keynesians put more weight on spending and demand.
Milton Friedman argued that 'inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon'.

title: The consumer price index basket
description: The CPI tracks the cost of a representative, spending-weighted basket of goods and services, which is updated as habits change.

facts.text: The consumer price index (CPI) tracks the cost of a representative basket of goods and services households buy; its rise measures inflation.
For the US CPI, data collectors record the prices of about 80,000 items every month.
Each item in the CPI basket is weighted by how much households actually spend on it, based on surveys of what they buy.
Housing is the largest part of the US CPI basket, far bigger than clothing.
In 2024, the UK's inflation basket held 744 items, and its contents and weights are updated every year.
In 2024, the UK added air fryers to its inflation basket, for their energy savings, and vinyl records returned after over thirty years.
In 2024, hand sanitiser was dropped from the UK's inflation basket as its shelf space shrank after the pandemic.

title: Why a fixed basket overstates living costs
description: Substitution bias and quality/new goods bias make a fixed-basket index overstate the rise in the cost of living.

facts.text: A fixed basket overstates the rise in living costs because people switch away from goods whose prices rise: substitution bias.
A fixed basket also misses quality improvements and new goods, which likewise makes it overstate the rise in the cost of living.
By the early 2000s, US statisticians were using methods that allow for some switching between goods.

title: Hyperinflation and its causes
description: Hyperinflation is inflation above 50% a month, usually begun by governments creating money to pay for spending and fed by collapsing trust.

facts.text: In 1956, economist Phillip Cagan defined hyperinflation as monthly inflation above 50%.
Hyperinflations usually start when governments create new money to pay for spending, faster than the economy can produce.
As trust in the money collapses, people spend it faster and flee to foreign currencies, which pushes prices up even faster.

title: Weimar Germany's hyperinflation
description: In 1923, Germany printed money to pay its bills until a dollar cost trillions of marks; historians debate how much reparations were to blame.

facts.text: A US dollar cost just over four German marks in 1914; by late 1923, it cost about 4.2 trillion.
After World War I, Germany's government printed more and more money to pay its bills, including war reparations.
In early 1923, French and Belgian troops occupied Germany's Ruhr region and coal output there stopped, driving prices up further.
Germany's hyperinflation wiped out many people's savings.
Historians still debate how much blame lies with reparations and how much with Germany's own choices, such as printing rather than taxing.

title: Zimbabwe's hyperinflation
description: In 2008, after land reforms crippled farming and the government printed money, Zimbabwe's prices doubled roughly daily until it abandoned its currency in 2009.

facts.text: After land reforms crippled Zimbabwe's farm output, its government printed money aggressively.
At its peak in mid-November 2008, Zimbabwe's monthly inflation was about 79.6 billion percent, with prices doubling roughly every day.
In January 2009, Zimbabwe's central bank put a 100 trillion dollar note into circulation.
In 2009, Zimbabwe abandoned its own currency, and people used foreign money, mainly US dollars.

title: What deflation is
description: Deflation is a general fall in prices, usually a side effect of collapsing spending; falling prices in one sector are not deflation.

facts.text: In 2002, Fed governor Ben Bernanke defined deflation as a general decline in prices, stressing the word 'general'.
Prices falling in one sector because productivity is rising there are generally not a problem for the economy as a whole.
Deflation is almost always a side effect of a collapse in spending so severe that producers must keep cutting prices to find buyers.

title: Why deflation hurts
description: Falling prices lead people to delay purchases and raise the real burden of debts, which can slow an economy for years.

facts.text: When prices are falling, people delay purchases if they can, which means less economic activity, less income and slower growth.
When prices fall, borrowers must still repay the same amount of money, in dollars of ever-increasing real value.
By 2002, a mild fall in Japanese consumer prices, about 1% a year, had come with years of painfully slow growth.

title: What GDP measures
description: GDP is the market value of the final goods and services a country produces in a period; real GDP adjusts it for price changes.

facts.text: GDP measures the market value of the final goods and services produced in a country in a given period, such as a quarter or a year.
Only final products count in GDP: flour sold to a baker is an intermediate input, and the bread is the final product.
GDP can be added up three ways: value added at each stage of production, spending by final users, or incomes earned from production.
Real GDP adjusts GDP for price changes, so it shows growth in output rather than just rising prices.

title: What GDP misses
description: GDP leaves out unpaid work and ignores pollution, leisure and how income is shared; its pioneer Kuznets warned it is not a measure of welfare.

facts.text: GDP leaves out unpaid work, such as housework and volunteering, because it is hard to measure and value.
GDP also ignores environmental damage, lost leisure and how income is shared, so it is not a full measure of well-being.
In 1934, economist Simon Kuznets presented the first set of US national economic accounts in a report to Congress.
In that 1934 report, Kuznets warned that the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income.

title: Booms, recessions and how they are dated
description: Economies swing irregularly between expansions and recessions, marked by peaks and troughs; the NBER dates US recessions after the fact.

facts.text: Economies go through expansions, or booms, when activity grows, and recessions, when it declines.
Expansions and recessions come at irregular intervals and last for different lengths of time.
A peak is the last month of an expansion; a trough is the last month of a recession.
The NBER dates US recessions: a significant decline in economic activity, spread across the economy, lasting more than a few months.
Two straight quarters of falling real GDP is a popular rule of thumb, not the NBER's definition, though most recessions fit it.
On December 1, 2008, the NBER announced that a US recession had begun in December 2007.
The US recession of 2020 lasted about two months, from a peak in February to a trough in April.

title: What drives the business cycle
description: Economists disagree about what drives booms and recessions: swings in spending, interest-rate moves, or shocks to productivity and tastes.

facts.text: Many economists see spending swings as a main driver: a surge in private or public spending fuels a boom; a pullback brings a recession.
Central banks can also push the cycle, generating recessions or booms by raising or lowering interest rates.
Economists in the new classical tradition argue that cycles come largely from shocks to productivity and tastes, not changes in demand.
Economists still disagree about what drives business cycles.

title: How unemployment is measured
description: The US counts unemployment with a monthly household survey; the unemployed must lack a job, have looked for work and be available, and people outside the labor force are not counted.

facts.text: The US measures unemployment each month with the Current Population Survey, a survey of about 60,000 households.
People count as unemployed if they have no job, have actively looked for work in the prior 4 weeks, and are available to work.
Unemployment is not counted from benefit claims, because many jobless people are not eligible or never apply.
The labor force is everyone employed or unemployed; the unemployment rate is the unemployed as a percentage of the labor force.
Retirees, students and discouraged workers who have stopped looking are outside the labor force, so they are not counted as unemployed.

title: Frictional, structural and cyclical unemployment
description: Unemployment is frictional (between jobs), structural (skills mismatch) or cyclical (caused by recession); the first two make up the natural rate.

facts.text: Frictional unemployment happens while people move between jobs or look for their first one, so some always exists.
Structural unemployment happens when workers' skills no longer match what employers want, as when demand shifts away from those skills.
Cyclical unemployment rises during recessions and falls during expansions.
Frictional plus structural unemployment make up the natural rate, which exists even when the economy is neither booming nor in recession.

title: What a speculative bubble is
description: A bubble is a price far above what fundamentals justify for a long time, sustained by buyers expecting to sell higher; bubbles are hard to spot until they burst, and economists disagree about them.

facts.text: A bubble is when an asset's market price sits far above the price its fundamentals justify, for a long time.
In a bubble, buyers may pay above fundamental value because they expect to sell to someone even more optimistic.
Bubbles are hard to identify while they happen, and many are only seen as bubbles in hindsight.
In 2013, Robert Shiller, who says prices can drift from fundamentals, shared the economics Nobel with efficient-markets pioneer Eugene Fama.

title: Dutch tulip mania
description: The 1630s Dutch tulip craze, long called the first speculative bubble, crashed in February 1637; historian Anne Goldgar found it far smaller than legend says.

facts.text: Dutch tulip mania in the 1630s has long been considered the first recorded speculative bubble.
Collectors prized 'broken' tulips with striped petals; the stripes came from a virus that made those bulbs rare and unpredictable.
The Dutch tulip market cracked in February 1637, when many buyers said they couldn't pay the prices they had agreed.
Charles Mackay's 1841 book spread the story that everyone from rich merchants to chimney sweeps joined the tulip frenzy.
Historian Anne Goldgar searched the archives and found few people involved, minor damage, and nobody she could find who went bankrupt.

title: The dot-com bubble
description: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups; the Nasdaq peaked in March 2000 and fell more than 78% by October 2002.

facts.text: In the late 1990s, money poured into internet start-ups, many of them overvalued with little to show in products or profits.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index peaked in March 2000, and by October 2002 it had fallen more than 78% from its high.

title: The Great Depression and its legacy
description: The Great Depression (1929 to about 1941) was the deepest US downturn: output fell by a third, unemployment reached 25% and prices fell; it reshaped economic policy.

facts.text: The Great Depression lasted from 1929 until about 1941, the longest and deepest downturn in US history.
Between 1929 and 1933, US output fell by about a third and unemployment reached about 25% of the labor force.
Thousands of US banks failed during the Depression: more than 1,000 a year from 1930 to 1933.
US prices fell about 10% a year from 1930 to 1933.
The Depression brought federal deposit insurance, securities regulation, Social Security and the first national minimum wage.
The Depression sparked fundamental changes in economic institutions, economic policy and economic theory.
In 2002, Fed governor Ben Bernanke told Friedman and Schwartz: 'Regarding the Great Depression. You're right, we did it. We're very sorry.'
Bernanke's 2002 apology ended: 'But thanks to you, we won't do it again.'

title: What caused the Great Depression
description: Economists still disagree: the 1929 crash and falling spending, a shrinking money supply as banks failed (Friedman and Schwartz), and the gold standard all have advocates.

facts.text: Economists still disagree about what caused the Great Depression; there is no single agreed explanation.
The 1929 stock market crash destroyed wealth and sparked doubts that led consumers and firms to cut their spending.
Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued that a falling money stock, as banks failed, cut spending and drove down output and prices.
During the banking panics of 1930 to 1933, the Fed failed to act as lender of last resort, and the money supply fell by nearly 30%.
The gold standard helped spread the slump from country to country.

title: The 2008 financial crisis
description: A US housing bubble fed by risky mortgage lending burst, Lehman Brothers failed in 2008, and the Great Recession followed; economists still debate the causes.

facts.text: US home prices more than doubled between 1998 and 2006, the sharpest rise in US history.
In the mid-2000s, risky mortgages were packaged into securities, widening access to credit and pushing up house prices.
US home prices fell by over a fifth on average from early 2007 to mid-2011, leading to mortgage defaults and foreclosures.
In September 2008, the investment bank Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy, and the crisis spread through the financial system.
The Great Recession lasted 18 months, from December 2007 to June 2009, the longest US recession since World War II.
During the Great Recession, US unemployment more than doubled, from under 5% to 10%.
In the 12 months to March 2009, US consumer prices fell 0.4%, the first such decline since 1955.
John Taylor blamed the housing boom on the Fed keeping rates low too long; Bernanke said that explains little, citing a global savings glut.

title: Gains from trade
description: Voluntary trade happens only when both sides expect to gain, but a country's gains are spread widely while some workers and firms lose.

facts.text: For a voluntary trade to happen, it must make both parties better off, which makes trade a positive-sum game.
People trade because it makes them better off, in a school cafeteria or in the global marketplace.
Trade gives consumers lower prices and more variety and exporters bigger markets, but some firms fail against foreign rivals and their workers lose jobs.
Trade's gains are spread widely and are hard to see, while its costs land on specific companies and workers.

title: Why countries make different things
description: Countries differ in resources, climate and skills, so each can make some things far more cheaply than others and trade for the rest.

facts.text: Adam Smith wrote that very good wine could be made in Scotland with glass, hotbeds and heated walls, at about 30 times the cost of importing it.
Countries have different natural advantages: Chile has copper and Guatemala's climate suits coffee, so Chile provides copper, Guatemala coffee, and they trade.
Exports bring money into a country, and imports send money out of it.

title: Comparative advantage
description: A country has a comparative advantage in a good it makes at a lower cost in terms of the other goods it gives up; specializing by comparative advantage lets both sides gain.

facts.text: A country has an absolute advantage in a good if it can produce more of it than another country with the same resources.
A country has a comparative advantage in a good when it can produce it at a lower cost in terms of the other goods it gives up.
Comparative advantage gets more complex in real life, once limited resources and the state of a country's labor and jobs are counted.

title: Ricardo's wine and cloth
description: In 1817, David Ricardo showed that Portugal and England both gain by specializing and trading, even though Portugal made both wine and cloth with fewer workers.

facts.text: In 1817, David Ricardo argued that specialization and free trade benefit all trading partners, even relatively inefficient ones.
In Ricardo's example, England needs 100 workers for a year to make its cloth and 120 for its wine; Portugal needs 90 for the cloth and 80 for the wine.
If Portugal makes only wine and England only cloth and they trade, each can consume more wine and more cloth than by making both itself.

title: Imports and exports
description: Exports are goods and services sold abroad and imports are those bought from abroad; services, including travel spending, count too.

facts.text: Exports are goods and services a country sells to other countries; imports are goods and services it buys from them.
Countries trade services such as finance, software, consulting and design, not only goods.
What foreign visitors spend in a country counts as that country's exports; what its residents spend on trips abroad counts as imports.

title: The balance of trade
description: The trade balance is exports minus imports: a surplus if exports are bigger, a deficit if imports are; whether deficits matter is debated.

facts.text: The trade balance is exports minus imports: a country that exports more than it imports runs a trade surplus, and one that imports more runs a trade deficit.
The United States has run a trade deficit year after year since the mid-1970s.
Some policymakers see a trade deficit as proof a country is losing at trade; most experts say a deficit or surplus is in itself neither good nor bad.

title: Tariffs and who pays them
description: A tariff is a tax on imports paid by the importing company; the cost can pass to consumers, be absorbed, or squeeze foreign exporters.

facts.text: A tariff is a tax on goods as they cross a national border, usually charged by the importing country's government.
The importing company, not the foreign country, pays the tariff to the customs authority.
Importers can pass tariff costs on to shoppers as higher prices or absorb them, and foreign exporters may accept lower profit margins.
After US tariffs on imported washing machines in early 2018, washer prices rose about 12%, and dryers, which had no tariff, rose by a similar amount.
Washers and dryers are often bought together, so sellers facing the washer tariff raised dryer prices too.

title: The tariff debate
description: Supporters say tariffs protect industries, jobs and national security; critics say they raise costs, distort markets and invite retaliation.

facts.text: The 2018 washer tariffs created about 1,800 US jobs, at a yearly cost to consumers of roughly $815,000 per job (Flaaen, Hortaçsu and Tintelnot).
Supporters say tariffs protect domestic industries, preserve jobs and bolster national security.
Governments also use tariffs to raise revenue and as political leverage.
The infant-industry argument is to block imports for a limited time so a young industry can grow up before facing full competition.
Critics say tariffs distort markets, raise costs and provoke retaliation from trading partners.

title: Exchange rates
description: An exchange rate is the price of one currency in terms of another, set in the foreign exchange market; a stronger currency makes imports cheaper and exports dearer.

facts.text: Foreign exchange trading averaged $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025, up from $7.5 trillion in 2022.
The foreign exchange market is where people and firms use one currency to buy another.
An exchange rate is how much one currency is worth in terms of another.
Tourists, firms that trade across borders and investors buying assets abroad all buy and sell currencies.
A currency that buys more of another than before has appreciated, or strengthened; one that buys less has depreciated, or weakened.
A stronger dollar helps Americans buying imports or traveling abroad; a weaker dollar helps US exporters and foreign tourists visiting the US.

title: Why exchange rates move
description: Floating exchange rates move with supply and demand for a currency, driven by interest rates, inflation and expectations; some countries fix their rates instead.

facts.text: A floating exchange rate is mainly set by the market, through supply of and demand for the currency.
Relatively high interest rates attract funds from abroad, raising demand for a country's currency and tending to push it up.
Relatively high inflation erodes a currency's buying power, which tends to make it depreciate.
If people expect a currency to rise, they buy it, which can push its value up.
Under a fixed, or pegged, exchange rate, a country holds its currency's value steady against another currency.

title: The Silk Road
description: The Silk Road linked China with the West by caravan, with goods passing in stages through middlemen.

facts.text: The Silk Road was a caravan route of about 6,400 km linking China with the West, carrying goods and ideas between China and Rome.
On the Silk Road, silk went west while wool, gold and silver went east, and religions and diseases traveled it too.
Few people traveled the whole Silk Road; goods moved along it in stages, handled by middlemen.
After it became unsafe and little traveled, the Silk Road was revived under the Mongols, when Marco Polo traveled it.

title: Container shipping
description: Malcolm McLean's 1956 container voyage showed that loading whole boxes, rather than loose cargo, made shipping far cheaper.

facts.text: Before containers, loose break-bulk cargo could take several days to load, so ships often sat in port for long periods.
On April 26, 1956, trucking entrepreneur Malcolm McLean's ship Ideal X left Newark for Houston carrying 58 metal containers.
In 1956, loading a ship the conventional way cost more than $5.80 a ton; loading the Ideal X's containers cost about 16 cents a ton.

title: Global supply chains
description: Many products are made from parts and services sourced in many countries, so trade statistics and single disruptions can mislead or ripple worldwide.

facts.text: The container ship Ever Given ran aground in the Suez Canal on March 23, 2021, and was refloated on March 29.
The Suez Canal blockage held up about $9 billion of global trade each day.
About half of global trade takes place within global supply chains, which build products from parts and services sourced around the world.
The iPhone 3G's parts came from firms in Japan, South Korea, Germany and the US, and were assembled in China.
Assembly in China added about $6.50 to an iPhone 3G that cost $178.96 to make, about 3.6% of the total (Xing and Detert, 2010).
Trade statistics counted the whole $178.96 as a Chinese export when an iPhone 3G was shipped to the US.

title: The globalization debate
description: Globalization has lowered prices and helped poor countries grow, while job losses from import competition have been concentrated in particular places.

facts.text: Globalization lets countries specialize, which lowers the prices of goods and services.
More open economies helped once extremely poor countries grow faster and reduce poverty.
Economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found that by 2011, cheap Chinese imports had cost the US about 2.4 million jobs.
The China shock's job losses were concentrated in particular places, which saw persistently lower employment and earnings.
While workers in many US places lost their livelihoods to the China shock, consumers nationwide got slightly cheaper goods.

title: Institutions and the wealth of nations
description: Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson link prosperity to institutions: inclusive rules support growth, extractive ones enrich an elite.

facts.text: Nogales is cut in half by the US–Mexico border fence; people in Nogales, Arizona, are generally much better off than those in Nogales, Sonora.
The two halves of Nogales share a climate, many ancestors, food and music, so the laureates argue the difference is institutions, not geography or culture.
The richest 20% of the world's countries are about 30 times richer than the poorest 20%.
The poorest countries have become richer, but they are not catching up with the most prosperous.
Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson and James Robinson won the 2024 economics Nobel for studies of how institutions are formed and affect prosperity.
Inclusive institutions, with secure property rights and the rule of law, support long-run growth; extractive ones benefit a small elite at others' expense.

title: Other explanations for rich and poor countries
description: Other economists stress geography, disease and isolation, and all explanations meet at productivity: output per worker.

facts.text: Economist Jeffrey Sachs argued in 2003 that institutions matter, but not for everything: disease such as malaria and geographic isolation also hold poor countries back.
Labor productivity, the value each worker produces, rises with education and better technology, and it underpins a country's standard of living.

title: The IMF and the World Bank
description: The 1944 Bretton Woods conference created the IMF, which lends to countries in crisis with conditions, and the World Bank, which funds development.

facts.text: In July 1944, a year before World War II ended, delegates from 44 nations met at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire.
The Bretton Woods conference created the International Monetary Fund and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, now the World Bank.
The IMF was set up to watch over exchange rates and lend to countries short of foreign currency to pay their international bills.
Countries that borrow from the IMF agree to adjust their economic policies to overcome the problems that led them to seek help.
Critics argue that austere IMF loan conditions can reduce growth, worsen crises and hurt the poorest people.
The World Bank's first loan went to France for postwar rebuilding; when the Marshall Plan took over in Europe, the Bank turned to power, irrigation and transport.
Today, part of the World Bank gives grants and low-interest loans to help low-income countries invest and develop.

title: The World Trade Organization
description: The WTO, founded in 1995 from the 1947 GATT, sets trade rules, hosts negotiations and settles disputes between its members.

facts.text: The World Trade Organization began on 1 January 1995, succeeding the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT) of 1947.
The WTO runs trade agreements, hosts trade negotiations and handles trade disputes between its members.
The WTO has 166 members, which together account for 98% of world trade.
Critics say the WTO favors large corporations and raise concerns about its effects on the environment, labor rights and national sovereignty.

title: The Big Mac index and purchasing power parity
description: The Economist's Big Mac index compares burger prices to test purchasing power parity, the idea that exchange rates drift toward equalizing prices.

facts.text: The Economist created the Big Mac index in 1986 as a lighthearted way to illustrate purchasing power parity.
Purchasing power parity is the idea that exchange rates should move toward the rate that makes the same goods cost the same in different countries.
If a Big Mac costs less abroad, in dollars, than in the US, the index suggests that currency may be undervalued; if it costs more, overvalued.
The Big Mac index can't fully account for local wages, taxes and other costs of doing business, and one burger can't represent a whole economy.

title: Ways to own a business
description: A sole proprietorship has one owner and a partnership two or more; in both, owners are personally liable for the business's debts. A corporation is a separate legal entity whose owners have limited liability.

facts.text: A sole proprietorship is a business owned by one person, who has unlimited personal liability for all of its debts.
In a partnership, two or more people own a business together, and in a general partnership every partner faces unlimited personal liability.
A corporation is a legal entity separate from its owners: it can own property, enter into contracts, and sue and be sued.
With limited liability, a corporation's owners can lose no more than the amount they invested in it.

title: Salomon and the company as a separate person
description: In the Salomon case, Britain's House of Lords ruled that a properly formed company is a separate person in law, so its owner was not personally liable for its debts.

facts.text: In 1892, Aron Salomon, a leather boot maker in Whitechapel, London, turned the business he had run as a sole proprietor into a limited company, keeping nearly all of its shares.
Salomon's company soon failed owing money. Its liquidator argued that Salomon should be personally liable, but the House of Lords ruled that the company was a separate person in law.

title: Who runs a corporation
description: Shareholders own a corporation and elect a board of directors, which sets goals and policies and hires officers such as the CEO to run the firm.

facts.text: In a corporation, shareholders elect a board of directors, which sets major goals and policies and hires officers, such as the chief executive officer (CEO), to run the firm.

title: Entrepreneurs and the risk of starting up
description: An entrepreneur organizes, runs and carries the risk of a business. HP began in a garage with $538; about half of new US businesses close within five years.

facts.text: An entrepreneur is a person who organizes, manages and takes on the risk of a business; the word comes from the Old French entreprendre, "to undertake".
Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard began part-time work in a Palo Alto garage with $538 in working capital, including the value of Packard's used drill press.
California has made the HP garage a state historical landmark, the "Birthplace of Silicon Valley".
On January 1, 1939, Hewlett and Packard formalized their partnership, and they chose the company's name with a coin toss.
Of US business establishments that opened in March 2013, 79.6% were still operating after one year, 50.6% after five years and 34.7% after ten.

title: Start-up costs and funding
description: Starting a business involves one-time costs (equipment, permits, licenses) and ongoing ones (rent, salaries, utilities), usually funded by savings, loans or investors who take a share of ownership.

facts.text: Start-up costs include one-time expenses, such as major equipment, permits and licenses, and ongoing ones, such as rent, salaries and utilities.
New businesses are commonly funded by the founders' own savings, by loans, or by investors who put in money in return for a share of ownership.

title: Revenue, costs and profit
description: Revenue is what a business takes in from sales (price times quantity); profit is revenue minus total cost, and a loss when costs are bigger. Amazon sold billions and still lost money in 2002.

facts.text: A firm's total revenue is the income it gets from selling its products: the price times the quantity sold.
Profit is total revenue minus total cost; when costs are bigger than revenue, the result is a loss.
In 2002, Amazon had net sales of about $3.9 billion but a net loss of about $149 million.
In 2003, Amazon made its first full-year profit: about $35 million on net sales of about $5.26 billion.

title: Fixed and variable costs
description: Fixed costs, such as rent, machinery and advertising, stay the same however much a firm produces; variable costs, such as labor and raw materials, rise and fall with output.

facts.text: Fixed costs, such as rent on a factory or shop, machinery and advertising, stay the same however much a firm produces.
Variable costs, such as labor and raw materials, rise and fall with how much a firm produces.

title: Economies of scale
description: Making more of something can lower the cost of each unit, mainly because fixed costs are spread over more units. Ford's mass-produced Model T fell from $850 to as little as $260.

facts.text: Average cost is total cost divided by the number of units produced, and it falls as fixed costs are spread over more output.
Economies of scale occur when the cost per unit falls as the quantity produced goes up.
From 1908 to 1927, Ford built more than 15 million Model Ts, and the price dropped from $850 to as little as $260.
Mass production let Ford sell the Model T cheaply, and by the early 1920s more than half of the registered cars in the world were Fords.

title: Diseconomies of scale
description: A firm can grow so large that it becomes hard to manage, and then its cost per unit rises again.

facts.text: Diseconomies of scale happen when a firm grows so large it is hard to manage: layers of managers struggle to communicate, work gets disrupted, and cost per unit rises.

title: The division of labor and the pin factory
description: In The Wealth of Nations (1776), Adam Smith showed that splitting pin-making into about 18 operations let ten workers make upwards of 48,000 pins a day, and explained why specializing raises output.

facts.text: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, opens with a chapter on the division of labour.
In Smith's pin factory, making a pin was divided into about 18 distinct operations: one worker draws out the wire, another straightens it, a third cuts it, and so on.
Smith described ten workers who, by dividing the operations, could make upwards of 48,000 pins a day, about 4,800 each.
Working alone, Smith wrote, each worker could certainly not make 20 pins a day, and perhaps not even one.
Smith gave three reasons dividing work raises output: workers grow more skilled at one task, they lose no time switching tasks, and it leads to machines that save labour.

title: Smith's warning about repetitive work
description: Smith also warned that a lifetime of a few simple, repeated operations could dull a worker's mind.

facts.text: In Book V, Smith warned that a worker who spends a whole life performing a few simple operations "generally becomes as stupid and ignorant as it is possible for a human creature to become".

title: Wages as the price of labor
description: A wage is the price of labor, set in a labor market where employers demand and workers supply labor. More productive workers are in more demand, and jobs needing long training have fewer candidates.

facts.text: In a labor market, the wage or salary is the price of labor: employers demand workers, and workers supply their labor.
Employers' demand for workers rises when those workers are more productive, for example better trained, and when demand rises for the products they make.
Jobs that need more education or training have a smaller supply of qualified workers.
In 2024, US full-time workers aged 25 and over with a bachelor's degree had median weekly earnings of $1,543, compared with $930 for those with only a high school diploma.

title: Compensating differentials
description: Dirty, dangerous or unpleasant jobs tend to pay more than pleasant jobs needing similar skill. Adam Smith noticed it; economists call it a compensating differential.

facts.text: Adam Smith wrote that wages vary with the ease or hardship, the cleanliness or dirtiness, and the honourableness of a job.
Smith noted that a journeyman blacksmith seldom earned in 12 hours what a coal miner earned in 8, because mining was dirtier, more dangerous and done underground.
Economists call the extra pay needed to attract workers to dangerous or unpleasant jobs a compensating differential.

title: Unions and collective bargaining
description: A union is an association of workers acting together to improve their conditions. It negotiates with employers through collective bargaining and can strike. About 1 in 10 US workers is a member.

facts.text: A labor union is an association of workers that tries to improve working conditions through collective action.
Collective bargaining is negotiation between workers' representatives and employers to set the conditions of employment, such as wages, hours and working conditions.
A strike is a collective refusal by employees to work under the conditions their employer requires.
In the US, 10.0% of wage and salary workers (about 1 in 10) were union members in 2025, down from 20.1% in 1983.

title: The Flint sit-down strike
description: In 1936 and 1937, autoworkers occupied General Motors plants in Flint, Michigan, for 44 days until GM recognized their union, the United Auto Workers.

facts.text: The Flint sit-down strike against General Motors lasted 44 days, from December 30, 1936, to February 11, 1937.
The Flint strikers occupied GM's plants instead of picketing outside, which protected them from the weather and from being replaced by other workers.
On February 11, 1937, General Motors agreed to recognize the strikers' union, the United Auto Workers (UAW).
Sit-down strikes are now counted among illegal kinds of strike.

title: The Luddites
description: From 1811, English textile workers known as Luddites smashed machines. They objected less to machines than to how owners used them to undercut skilled, fairly paid work.

facts.text: The Luddite protests began near Nottingham, England, in March 1811, when workers smashed knitting machines called stocking frames.
The Luddites claimed to follow "Ned Ludd", a leader who never existed, and used his name to sign threatening letters.
The Luddites were not against machines as such; they objected to owners using machines to get around labor standards, with cheaper, lower-quality work.
Parliament made machine-breaking a capital crime.

title: How automation reshapes jobs
description: Machines take over tasks, but work often shifts rather than vanishing: US farm jobs fell from 41% of the workforce to 1.9%, and ATMs changed tellers' work instead of ending it.

facts.text: The share of the US workforce employed in agriculture fell from 41% in 1900 to 1.9% in 2000, as tractors replaced horses and mules.
More productive farms freed a large share of the population for jobs outside farming.
As ATMs spread, tellers per urban bank branch fell from 20 to 13 between 1988 and 2004, but banks opened 43% more urban branches, so teller jobs did not disappear.
Tellers' work shifted away from handling cash toward helping customers with other services.
In 1961, Unimate, the first industrial robot, went to work at a General Motors plant, lifting and stacking hot die-cast metal parts.

title: Advertising that informs
description: Advertising can tell buyers what exists and what it costs. Lee Benham found eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising.

facts.text: Economist Lee Benham found in 1972 that eyeglasses cost more in US states that banned advertising than in states that allowed it.
Advertising gives buyers information about products and their prices, which helps them compare.

title: Advertising that persuades
description: Advertising also shapes preferences: people with strong ketchup favorites often cannot tell brands apart blindfolded, and De Beers's "A Diamond Is Forever" helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring.

facts.text: Many people cannot tell common ketchups or mayonnaises apart blindfolded, yet past habits and advertising give them strong brand preferences.
Copywriter Frances Gerety of the agency N. W. Ayer wrote "A Diamond Is Forever" for De Beers in 1947.
In 1999, Advertising Age named "A Diamond Is Forever" the best advertising slogan of the 20th century.
The campaign helped make the diamond solitaire the standard engagement ring; earlier engagement rings often used colored gems, small diamonds or pearls.

title: Rival advertising can cancel out
description: A. C. Pigou argued in 1920 that when competing firms advertise against each other, the spending may simply cancel out.

facts.text: In 1920, economist A. C. Pigou argued that rival firms' advertising may simply cancel out, leaving each as it would have been if neither had advertised.

title: Why firms exist (Coase)
description: Ronald Coase argued in 1937 that firms exist because using markets has costs, now called transaction costs, such as finding prices and negotiating a contract for each deal. Inside a firm, managers direct the work.

facts.text: In his 1937 paper "The Nature of the Firm", Ronald Coase asked why firms exist at all if markets can coordinate work.
Coase's answer: using markets has costs, such as discovering prices and negotiating a separate contract for each deal, now called transaction costs.
Inside a firm, work is directed by managers instead of being arranged through prices and a separate contract for each task.
Coase won the 1991 Nobel Prize in economics, partly for showing why transaction costs matter for how the economy is organized.

title: Adam Smith's invisible hand
description: Smith's idea that many people pursuing their own interest through trade can produce outcomes that benefit society, though no one intends them.

facts.text: Scottish philosopher Adam Smith published The Wealth of Nations in 1776.
Smith wrote that we expect our dinner not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer or the baker, but from their regard to their own interest.
The invisible hand is Smith's metaphor for how good social and economic outcomes can arise from many self-interested actions, none meant to produce them.
Smith used the phrase 'invisible hand' only once in The Wealth of Nations, and once in The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759).
Smith wrote that a person who 'intends only his own gain' is 'led by an invisible hand to promote an end which was no part of his intention.'
The invisible hand has also been used, more controversially, to argue that free markets deliver the best possible outcomes.

title: Smith's limits and critics
description: Smith gave government real duties and distrusted collusion among traders; modern critics such as Joseph Stiglitz argue the invisible hand often fails.

facts.text: Smith gave government three duties: defense, justice, and public works like roads and bridges that help society but would not pay a private builder.
Smith warned that people of the same trade seldom meet without the talk ending in a conspiracy against the public or a scheme to raise prices.
In 2002, economist Joseph Stiglitz wrote that the invisible hand is invisible, at least in part, because it is not there.

title: Marx's critique of capitalism
description: Marx argued that labor creates value, that owners keep the surplus as profit, and that class struggle would end in the overthrow of capitalism.

facts.text: Karl Marx published The Communist Manifesto with Friedrich Engels in 1848, and the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867.
Marx built on concepts inherited from earlier economists, including Adam Smith and David Ricardo.
The labor theory of value holds that a product's value is set by the amount of labor needed to make it.
Marx argued that owners pay workers less than the value their labor adds, usually just enough to live on, and keep the rest, surplus value, as profit.
Marx saw history as a series of class struggles; under capitalism, between owners of capital and workers.
Marx and Engels predicted that the industrial working class would one day overthrow capitalism.
Marx expected capitalism to concentrate wealth in fewer hands.
Marx expected revolution in industrialized countries; Lenin's version stressed peasants in mostly agrarian societies such as Russia.

title: Marx's reach and his critics
description: Marx's ideas inspired communist governments ruling about a third of the world, while critics such as the Austrian school rejected the labor theory of value.

facts.text: For much of the 20th century, about a third of the world's population lived under communist governments.
Leaders including Lenin and Mao built on Marx's writings to impose communism on more than twenty countries.
The Austrian school argued that a thing's value comes from its ability to satisfy wants, not the labor used to make it.
Linking value to labor has proved hard to measure, because labor varies in skill and training.
Marx's ideas also inspired labor and socialist movements in western Europe.

title: Keynes and spending in a slump
description: Keynes argued that unemployment comes from too little total spending, and that government should spend, even by borrowing, to fill the gap.

facts.text: John Maynard Keynes published The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money in 1936.
Keynes's theory centers on total spending in the economy, called aggregate demand.
In Keynes's view, businesses won't hire workers to make goods that can't be sold, so unemployment comes from too little demand.
Keynes argued that cutting wages would not cure unemployment; government should raise spending and run a budget deficit.
Keynes wrote that burying banknotes in bottles in old coal mines for firms to dig up would end unemployment, though building houses would be more sensible.

title: Keynes's legacy and critics
description: Keynes helped design Bretton Woods and dominated Western policy until the 1970s, when monetarists led by Milton Friedman gained ground; Hayek never accepted his case.

facts.text: At the 1944 Bretton Woods conference, Keynes was one of the architects of the postwar system of fixed exchange rates.
Keynesian economics guided most Western governments until the 1970s, when monetarism eclipsed it.
Monetarists, led by Milton Friedman, argued government should steady the economy only by growing the money supply at a steady rate.
Most economists believe Keynes won his 1930s debate with Friedrich Hayek, but Hayek never believed it.

title: Market, command and mixed economies
description: In a market economy decisions are spread among buyers and sellers; in a command economy goals come from rulers; most real economies mix the two.

facts.text: In a market economy, decision-making is spread out among buyers and sellers, and it rests on private enterprise.
In a command economy, economic effort serves goals handed down from a ruler or ruling class.
Most economies in the real world are mixed, combining elements of market and command systems.
The Soviet Union's planning board, Gosplan, turned the party's goals into national plans, starting its first Five-Year Plan in 1928.
The inefficiency of communist economies played a large part in the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.
Even market economies rely on government rules that protect property, enforce contracts, prevent fraud and collect taxes.

title: Hayek and prices as signals
description: Hayek argued that the knowledge an economy needs is scattered among many people, and that prices pass it along in a way no central planner could.

facts.text: Friedrich Hayek set out his argument in 'The Use of Knowledge in Society', published in 1945.
Hayek argued that the knowledge an economy needs exists in no single mind; each person knows things about their own resources that a planner never can.
In Hayek's tin example, tens of thousands of tin users need not know why it became scarce; with no order given, the price tells them to use less.
Hayek described the price system as a kind of telecommunications system.

title: Loss aversion and the endowment effect
description: People tend to feel losses more strongly than equal gains, so owners value things more than non-owners: the endowment effect, shown in the 1990 mug experiment.

facts.text: In a 1990 experiment by Thaler, Kahneman and Knetsch, randomly chosen people got mugs they could sell; theory predicted about half would trade, but far fewer did.
Traditional economic theory assumes people have good information and can process it perfectly.
Psychologist Daniel Kahneman won the 2002 economics Nobel for bringing psychological research into economics.
Kahneman's work with Amos Tversky included 'Prospect Theory', published in 1979.
Loss aversion is the tendency to feel a loss more strongly than an equally large gain.
Thaler explained the endowment effect, valuing something more once you own it, through loss aversion.
In 2003, economist John List found that as traders gained market experience, the endowment effect faded.

title: Mental accounting
description: Thaler's idea that people sort money into separate accounts in their heads and judge each decision on its own.

facts.text: Mental accounting describes how people sort money into separate accounts in their heads and judge each decision on its own.
Losing feels less painful if you're still 'in the black' in that mental account, which Thaler calls the house money effect.
Richard Thaler won the 2017 economics Nobel for his contributions to behavioral economics.

title: The prisoner's dilemma
description: A game in which each player does better by betraying whatever the other does, yet both end up worse off than if both had cooperated.

facts.text: When two shopkeepers each cut prices to win customers, neither gains customers and both earn smaller profits.
In the prisoners' dilemma, both silent means 1 year each, both confessing 5 years each; a lone confessor goes free and the silent one gets 20 years.
Whatever the other suspect does, each does better by confessing, yet both confessing is worse for each than both staying silent.
Merrill Flood and Melvin Dresher devised the game at the RAND Corporation in 1950; Albert Tucker later added the prison story.
In an arms race, two nations keep buying weapons; neither gains an advantage and both end up poorer.

title: Cooperation in repeated games
description: When a game repeats with no known last round, cooperation can pay; tit for tat, which cooperates first and then copies, did well in Axelrod's tournaments.

facts.text: When the game repeats and players don't know which round is last, cooperation can emerge.
In Robert Axelrod's tournaments, Anatol Rapoport's tit for tat, cooperate first and then copy the partner's last move, did famously well.
Axelrod found that every 'nice' strategy, one that never betrays first, beat every strategy that wasn't nice.

title: The Gini coefficient
description: A single number from 0 (everyone has the same) to 1 (one person has everything) that measures how unequally income is shared.

facts.text: Italian statistician Corrado Gini devised the Gini coefficient in 1912.
A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality; 1 means one person gets all the income and everyone else none.
The Gini is tied to the Lorenz curve, a 1905 chart of what share of income goes to what share of people.
The Gini shows how unequal a distribution is but not why; two countries with very different income patterns can share a score.
Some countries measure consumption rather than income, which can miss how much wealth the richest households hold.

title: Wealth versus income inequality
description: Income is a flow of money coming in; wealth is a stock of what you own. Wealth is far more unequally shared than income.

facts.text: Wealth is a stock of resources you own; income is a flow of money coming in.
Across 28 OECD countries, the richest 10% of households held 52% of household wealth; the top 10% of earners got 24% of income.
On average, wealth inequality across OECD countries is about twice the level of income inequality.

title: Externalities
description: An externality is the effect of a deal on a third party outside it; when costs like pollution are ignored, markets make too much of the product.

facts.text: An externality is the effect of a market exchange on a third party who is outside the exchange.
An outdoor concert's noise affects neighbors who had no part in buying the tickets.
Pollution is a negative externality: a producer's costs cover labor and materials, but not the harm its pollution does to others.
When firms don't pay for the pollution they cause, the market produces too much of the product.
Externalities can be positive too; research and development is a standard example.

title: Pigou's tax on externalities
description: In 1920, Arthur Pigou proposed taxing activities that impose costs on others and subsidizing those that spread benefits; a carbon tax is a modern example.

facts.text: Economist Arthur Pigou's most influential work was The Economics of Welfare, published in 1920.
Pigou argued that negative externalities should be offset by a tax and positive externalities by a subsidy.
A carbon tax is a modern Pigouvian tax, ideally set equal to the social cost of carbon.

title: Coase and bargaining over externalities
description: Ronald Coase argued in 1960 that when deals cost little to make, affected parties can bargain to an efficient fix without government.

facts.text: Ronald Coase challenged Pigou's approach in his 1960 paper 'The Problem of Social Cost'.
Coase's example: a rancher whose cattle damage a neighbor's crops, and a farmer who could pay the rancher to keep fewer cattle.
Coase showed that if deals cost little to make, the parties can bargain to an efficient outcome without government, whoever the law favors.
The costs of making a deal vary from negligible to enormous.
Coase won the 1991 economics Nobel for his work on transaction costs and property rights.

title: Keynes's 15-hour week
description: In 1930, Keynes predicted much higher living standards and a 15-hour work week a century later; longer lives and retirements delivered extra leisure instead.

facts.text: In 1930, Keynes predicted living standards four to eight times higher a century later, and a 15-hour work week.
Economist Nicholas Crafts concluded that Keynes's 15-hour week will not arrive by 2030.
UK expected lifetime hours of leisure and home production rose 58% from 1931 to 2011, reflecting longer lives and longer retirements.

title: Nudges and defaults
description: Behavioral economics shows that details like the default option steer decisions; Thaler and Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow lets people commit now to save more later.

facts.text: Behavioral economists find that simple details, like the default option (what happens unless you choose otherwise), shape decisions.
Thaler and Shlomo Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow plan uses the fact that promising to save more in the future, especially after a raise, feels easier.
Some critics call such programs paternalistic; supporters stress that joining is voluntary and people can opt out at any time.

title: The sunk cost effect
description: The tendency to keep going with something because of money, effort or time already spent; Arkes and Blumer showed it with theater season tickets.

facts.text: The sunk cost effect is a greater tendency to keep going with something once money, effort or time has been invested in it.
In a 1985 study, theater-goers randomly charged full price for season tickets went to more plays over the next six months than those given discounts.
